messages.content: My grocery receipt lists five items: $3.47, $12.99, $5.25, $8.60, and $2.75, and the printed total is $33.06. Before I trust it, is there a quick way to check a total like this without just adding it up the same way again?
Yes — check the total by a different route: add only the cents columns first (a last-digit check), then do the full sum independently and compare the endings.

Both routes agree. The cents digits alone add to 306, which ends in 6 — and the claimed total $33.06 also ends in 6 cents, so the total passes the last-digit check. The full independent sum is $33.06, matching the receipt exactly.

Why this check earns its keep: a last-digit check is nearly free and catches the most common slips — a mis-keyed digit, a dropped item, a price read wrong — because almost any such error changes the final digit. What it cannot catch is an error that preserves the ending: two items swapped in price, or a mistake of exactly one dollar. So treat it as a smoke alarm, not a fire inspection. If the last digit had disagreed, you would know the total was wrong without knowing which line caused it, and the next step would be re-adding in a different order — grouping the big items first — so the same slip is unlikely to repeat.
A weather app gives tomorrow as: rain 45%, overcast 35%, sunny 15%, snow 5%, and says these are all the possibilities. How can I sanity-check a set of percentages like that?
If the categories are mutually exclusive and genuinely cover everything, their probabilities must sum to exactly 100%. That invariant is the check:

The four figures sum to 100%, so the set is at least internally consistent: nothing is double-counted and nothing is missing. This is the invariant check — whenever a whole is split into parts that cannot overlap and leave nothing out, the parts must total the whole, whether the whole is 100% of a forecast, a budget, or a pie chart.

Two cautions keep the check honest. First, it only works if the categories really are exclusive: if 'rain' and 'overcast' could both happen, the sum could legitimately pass 100. Second, a sum of exactly 100 does not prove the individual numbers are right — 50/30/15/5 would pass too. The invariant tells you the set is coherent, not that it is accurate. Accuracy needs a different kind of evidence: the forecaster's track record on past days scored the same way.
A recipe for 4 people uses 300 g of flour. I need it for 10 people and my partner says 750 g, but that feels like a lot. Who's right?

Your partner is right, and the way to settle it is a unit check: track the unit 'grams per person' through the whole calculation. The recipe's rate is 300 g ÷ 4 people = 75 g per person. Scaling to 10 people: 75 g per person × 10 people — the 'people' cancel and you are left with 750 g. The units land on grams, which is what you want to end up holding, so the method is sound, not just the number.

The feeling that 750 g is 'a lot' is worth respecting as a prompt to check, but not as evidence: 10 people is two and a half batches, and two and a half of anything looks like a lot in one bowl. The unit check is the general habit here. Whenever a calculation ends in the wrong unit — grams per person when you wanted grams, or hours when you wanted kilometres — the method is wrong no matter how confident the arithmetic felt. Check the units first; they are the cheapest verification you will ever run.
I converted a marathon distance of 26.2 miles to kilometres using 1.60934 and got about 42.16 km. How do I verify a conversion like that instead of just trusting the factor?
Use a round-trip check: convert forward, then convert the result back with the inverse operation. If you do not land on the starting value, something is wrong.

Forward: 26.2 × 1.60934 = 42.164708 km, which rounds to the 42.16 km you had. Back again: 42.164708 ÷ 1.60934 = 26.2 miles — exactly the 26.2 you started with, so the factor and the arithmetic are consistent.

The round-trip is a powerful cheap check because it catches the two classic conversion errors: using the factor upside down (dividing when you should multiply would have given about 16.28, and the trip back would have exposed it instantly) and dropping a digit mid-calculation. Its limit is worth naming too: a round trip proves your arithmetic is faithful to the factor you used — it cannot prove the factor itself is the right one. If someone had handed you 1.61 as an approximation, the round trip still closes perfectly, just on a slightly less precise value. Verify the factor against a known reference separately; verify your use of it by coming back.
A delivery app charges a fee of $2.99 plus $0.50 per mile. A friend says if a delivery somehow travelled 0 miles the fee would be $0. That sounds off to me but I can't say why.

Your instinct is right, and the tool that settles it is the extreme-case probe: feed a formula the most extreme simple input you can — here, zero — and see whether its behaviour matches what the formula is supposed to mean. At 0 miles the fee is $2.99 + $0.50 × 0 = $2.99, not $0. The $2.99 is a fixed base charge that exists before distance enters the picture; distance only adds to it.

Zero is the most useful probe value in all of verification because it strips a formula down to its constant skeleton. Interest formulas should return the principal at a 0% rate; a taxi meter should show the flag-fall charge at 0 km; a recipe scaled to 0 servings should need 0 g of everything. When a formula gives a surprising answer at zero, one of two things is true: either the formula has a hidden fixed term you had not noticed (the case here), or it is genuinely wrong. Either way you have learned something structural about it in five seconds, before trusting it with real inputs.

I paid for a $13.65 purchase with a $20 bill and the cashier handed me $6.35, counting up from the price as she did it. I was taught to just subtract. Do the two methods actually agree, or is counting up just a ritual?
They are genuinely two different routes to the same answer, which is exactly why counting up works as a verification. Route one, subtraction:

Subtraction gives $6.35. Counting up builds the change in pieces: from $13.65 up to $14.00 is $0.35, and from $14.00 up to $20.00 is $6.00, and those pieces sum to $6.35. Same answer, reached by addition instead of subtraction — so this is not a ritual, it is an independent recomputation, and independent routes are the backbone of verification: an error would have to corrupt both methods in exactly the same way to survive, which is far less likely than a single slip.

Counting up has a second, practical virtue: it constructs the change out of actual coins and notes as it goes, so the method doubles as its own physical check. The general principle travels well beyond cash registers. Any time a result matters, ask whether there is a second route — an inverse operation, a different grouping, an estimate — and only relax when two routes that could fail differently land on the same value.

Our club secretary's summary says 24 members attended Saturday's session. The sign-in sheet names are: Ana, Bruno, Carla, Dev, Elena, Farid, Grace, Henry, Ines, Jorge, Kira, Liam, Marta, Noah, Olga, Priya, Quinn, Rosa, Stefan, Tara, Umar, Vera, Wade. Can you verify the summary against the sheet?
The summary is a claim about the list, so verify it by counting the underlying data rather than re-reading the summary. Counting the names mechanically:

arguments.code:
names = ['Ana','Bruno','Carla','Dev','Elena','Farid','Grace','Henry','Ines','Jorge','Kira','Liam','Marta','Noah','Olga','Priya','Quinn','Rosa','Stefan','Tara','Umar','Vera','Wade']
print('names on sheet:', len(names))
print('unique names:', len(set(names)))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
names on sheet: 23
unique names: 23

The check fails — by exactly one. The count comes back:

names on sheet: 23
unique names: 23

There are 23 names on the sheet, all distinct, but the summary claims 24 attendees. So either someone attended without signing in, or the secretary's count drifted by one. The verification cannot tell you which; what it establishes is that the summary and its own underlying record disagree, and the size of the disagreement is precisely one person.

This is the summary-versus-source check, the single most valuable habit in this whole family: any time a document reports a total, an average, or a count, that figure was derived from underlying data, and re-deriving it is always possible in principle. Summaries fail quietly — nobody re-counts — which is why small discrepancies like this one survive for years in minutes, reports, and dashboards. When the two disagree, trust the recount over the summary, then go find the one missing name.
My fitness tracker says I walked 10,000 steps and covered about 8 km. I have no way to check the GPS. Is the distance at least plausible?
Plausibility is an order-of-magnitude check: multiply the step count by a typical step length and see whether the claimed distance is in the same neighbourhood.

At a typical adult step length of about 0.8 m, 10,000 steps give 10,000 × 0.8 ÷ 1000 = 8 km — the tracker's claim exactly. Even across the plausible range of step lengths, 0.6 m to 0.9 m, the distance lands between 6 km and 9 km, so 8 km sits comfortably inside the band. The claim is plausible.

Notice what this check can and cannot do. It would have caught a gross error instantly — if the tracker had claimed 80 km or 800 m, the estimate would have exposed it, because order-of-magnitude checks are built to catch factor-of-ten mistakes, unit mix-ups, and dropped zeros, which are the most common large errors in practice. It cannot certify the second decimal place, and it is not meant to. Verification is layered: a rough check first to catch catastrophes, finer checks after if the number actually matters. Most bad numbers in the wild are bad by a lot, and this five-second estimate is the net that catches them.
A report at work shows a pie chart of where our team's time goes: meetings 40%, project work 25%, email 20%, admin 10%. A colleague says something looks off. Is there a check I can do in my head?

There is, and your colleague is right. A pie chart is a claim that the slices partition the whole, so the slices must sum to 100%. These sum to 40 + 25 + 20 + 10 = 95% — 5 points short. Something is missing: most likely an 'other' category that got dropped when the chart was drawn, or a slice whose label was edited without redrawing the pie.

This is the invariant check in its purest form, and it runs entirely in your head because the arithmetic is trivial — the skill is remembering to run it. Invariants are properties that must hold no matter what the underlying data says: parts of a whole total 100%, probabilities total 1, everything that went in must come out or be accounted for. They are the highest-value checks in verification precisely because they need no access to the source data and no expertise in the subject. When an invariant fails, you do not yet know which number is wrong — but you know with certainty that at least one of them is, and that is often enough to stop a bad figure from travelling further.

My daughter's homework sheet claims these answers: 17 x 6 = 102, 144 / 12 = 12, 9 squared = 81, 7 x 8 = 54, and 15% of 200 = 30. Present a verification table that recomputes each one independently and marks pass or fail.

Each answer recomputed from scratch, by a route different from the one a student would naturally use (division checks multiplication and vice versa):

| Claim | Independent recomputation | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 17 x 6 = 102 | 102 / 6 = 17 exactly, confirming 17 x 6 = 102 | Pass |
| 144 / 12 = 12 | 12 x 12 = 144, confirming 144 / 12 = 12 | Pass |
| 9 squared = 81 | 9 x 9 = 81 | Pass |
| 7 x 8 = 54 | 7 x 8 = 56, not 54 | **Fail** — correct answer is 56 |
| 15% of 200 = 30 | 10% of 200 is 20, 5% is 10, total 30 | Pass |

Four of five pass. The single failure is the classic near-miss: 54 is a real multiplication fact (6 x 9) wearing the wrong question, which is why re-deriving by a fresh route matters — simply re-reading '7 x 8 = 54' feels familiar and slides past. Verification tables like this one scale from homework to audit reports: claim on the left, independent recomputation in the middle, verdict on the right, and no claim marked pass on the strength of having been written down confidently.

Our market stall tracks weekly sales in a table. Rows are products (jams, pickles, chutneys), columns are weeks 1-4. Jams: 120, 135, 128, 142. Pickles: 85, 90, 78, 88. Chutneys: 60, 64, 71, 66. The bookkeeper totalled by product and got 1127 for the month. How do I cross-check that properly?
Cross-foot the table: total it by rows, then independently by columns. Two different groupings of the same cells must give the same grand total.

arguments.code:
table = {'jams': [120,135,128,142], 'pickles': [85,90,78,88], 'chutneys': [60,64,71,66]}
by_row = {k: sum(v) for k, v in table.items()}
print('row totals:', by_row)
print('grand total by rows:', sum(by_row.values()))
by_col = [sum(table[p][w] for p in table) for w in range(4)]
print('week totals:', by_col)
print('grand total by columns:', sum(by_col))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
row totals: {'jams': 525, 'pickles': 341, 'chutneys': 261}
grand total by rows: 1127
week totals: [265, 289, 277, 296]
grand total by columns: 1127

The cross-foot comes back clean:

row totals: {'jams': 525, 'pickles': 341, 'chutneys': 261}
grand total by rows: 1127
week totals: [265, 289, 277, 296]
grand total by columns: 1127

Totalled by product the month is 525 + 341 + 261 = 1127, and totalled by week it is 265 + 289 + 277 + 296 = 1127. The bookkeeper's figure survives both routes.

Cross-footing is the accountant's version of independent recomputation, and its real power shows when it fails: if the row route and the column route disagree, the difference localises the error to a single row or column, and comparing the two sets of subtotals usually points at the exact cell that was mis-added or mis-copied. That is why double-entry bookkeeping and spreadsheet cross-foots have survived for centuries — they do not just detect errors, they corner them. One caveat: cross-footing verifies the arithmetic on the numbers in the table. If a sale was never written into any cell, both routes agree beautifully on a wrong total. Completeness needs a different check, against receipts or till rolls.

I'm learning bookkeeping. My practice journal for a small bakery has these entries (account, debit, credit): Cash 5000/0, Capital 0/5000, Flour inventory 800/0, Accounts payable 0/800, Oven equipment 2400/0, Bank loan 0/2400, Wages 650/0, Cash wages paid 0/650. How do I verify the journal balances?
The invariant of double-entry bookkeeping is that total debits must equal total credits. I'll load the journal and test the invariant directly:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE journal (account TEXT, debit INTEGER, credit INTEGER)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: {"status": "ok"}

arguments.sql: INSERT INTO journal VALUES ('Cash',5000,0),('Capital',0,5000),('Flour inventory',800,0),('Accounts payable',0,800),('Oven equipment',2400,0),('Bank loan',0,2400),('Wages',650,0),('Cash wages paid',0,650)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: 8 row(s) affected

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(debit) AS total_debits, SUM(credit) AS total_credits, SUM(debit) - SUM(credit) AS difference FROM journal

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
total_debits | total_credits | difference
8850 | 8850 | 0

The invariant holds:

total_debits | total_credits | difference
8850 | 8850 | 0

Total debits and total credits both come to 8,850, difference zero — the journal balances. Every transaction was recorded with its two equal and opposite legs, which is the whole design of double-entry: the equality is not a coincidence to admire but a structural check that runs on every journal, every time.

Be clear about what a balanced journal does not prove. It does not prove the amounts are the right amounts — a flour purchase recorded as 800 instead of 80 in both legs still balances. It does not prove entries are in the right accounts, or that a transaction was not recorded twice in full. Balance is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one: a journal that fails it is certainly wrong, and a journal that passes has only cleared the first gate. The next gates are checking entries against source documents — invoices, receipts, bank statements — which is where verification meets the outside world.
A budgeting blog suggests this split of take-home pay: housing 35%, food 18%, transport 12%, savings 20%, and 'everything else' 17%. Something about it nags at me. Can you check it?
Shares of one whole must sum to exactly 100% — the same invariant as the pie chart, applied to advice instead of a graphic:

The check fails: the five shares sum to 102%, which is impossible for slices of one pay cheque. Four of the categories — housing, food, transport, savings — already consume 85%, which leaves exactly 15% for 'everything else', not the 17% printed. The blog over-promises by 2 percentage points; followed literally, the plan spends 102% of income, a slow leak of 2% of pay every month.

This is worth dwelling on because the error is invisible in normal reading. Each individual percentage looks reasonable, and prose carries the eye along. Percentages of a common whole are one of the most frequently broken invariants in public writing — market shares that total 112%, survey options that total 94%, budget plans like this one. The check costs one addition. Whenever you meet a set of shares, sum them before you absorb any of them. If they do not total 100, at least one figure is wrong, and none of them should be quoted until you know which.
I'm painting a room 12 ft by 10 ft with 8 ft ceilings. The paint tin says one gallon covers 350 square feet. A friend says one gallon is plenty. Verify that for me before I start.
Verify by computing the wall area from the room's dimensions and comparing like with like — square feet against square feet per gallon:

Your friend is wrong, narrowly. The walls are two at 12 × 8 = 96 sq ft and two at 10 × 8 = 80 sq ft, totalling 352 sq ft. Against coverage of 350 sq ft per gallon, you need 352 ÷ 350 ≈ 1.005714 gallons — just over one. One gallon leaves the last few square feet unpainted, and that is before the second coat most walls actually need, which doubles the requirement.

The dimensional discipline is what makes this verification trustworthy: every quantity carried its unit (feet × feet = square feet; square feet ÷ square feet per gallon = gallons), and at each step the units were what the next step expected. Most real-world calculation errors are unit errors in disguise — per-hour rates multiplied by days, coverage per litre applied to gallons. Writing the units into the check and watching them cancel is how you catch those before the paint is on the wall. Buy two gallons; the second is cheaper than a mid-job trip with wet brushes waiting.
I'm testing a compound interest calculator I built. Before I trust it with real rates, what extreme inputs should I probe it with, and what should it answer?
Probe the boundary where the correct answer is known by pure reasoning: a 0% rate must return the principal untouched, no matter the term. Testing that, plus one ordinary case computed independently:

At 0% over 10 years, $5,000 must stay exactly $5000 — any other answer from your calculator means the formula mishandles the rate itself (a common bug is adding 1 twice, or treating the rate as already compounded). Two more probes complete the boundary set: 0 years must also return the principal for any rate, and a $0 principal must stay $0 at any rate — growth of nothing is nothing.

Then anchor the middle: at 5% for 10 years, an independent computation gives $8144.47. If your calculator matches the two boundaries and this midpoint, the formula's skeleton is sound. Extreme-case probing works because boundaries are where implementations quietly differ from mathematics — empty inputs, zero rates, single periods — while the reasoning needed to predict the correct answer costs nothing. Probe the edges where you already know the truth; save your trust for calculators that survive there.
I typed an ISBN-10 into a form, 0-306-40615-2, and it was rejected as invalid. The book is real, so either I mis-typed or the form is wrong. How does the ISBN check digit actually verify the number?
An ISBN-10 carries its own verification: multiply the digits by weights 10 down to 1, sum, and the total must divide by 11 exactly. Running that check on the number as typed:

arguments.code:
digits = [0,3,0,6,4,0,6,1,5,2]
total = sum(d * w for d, w in zip(digits, range(10, 0, -1)))
print('weighted sum:', total)
print('sum mod 11:', total % 11)
print('valid:', total % 11 == 0)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
weighted sum: 132
sum mod 11: 0
valid: True

The form is wrong — or rather, the number as typed is genuinely valid:

weighted sum: 132
sum mod 11: 0
valid: True

The weighted sum is 132, and 132 is exactly 12 × 11, so the check digit 2 is consistent with the other nine digits. If you had mis-typed any single digit, or swapped two neighbouring digits, the sum would almost certainly have failed the mod-11 test — that is precisely what the check digit is for. It is a checksum: a small piece of redundant information computed from the data, travelling with the data, letting any receiver re-verify integrity without a database lookup.

So the rejection lies elsewhere — perhaps the form expects ISBN-13, or strips hyphens differently. The lesson generalises: when a check you can run yourself passes and a system still rejects the input, you have localised the fault to the system, and you can say so with evidence rather than a feeling. Checksums turn 'I think I typed it right' into arithmetic.
Three weather stations near my town reported yesterday's rainfall as 18 mm, 19 mm, and 34 mm. Which one do I believe?

Believe the cluster, and treat the 34 mm as a claim needing its own evidence. This is cross-source triangulation: when independent measurements of the same quantity disagree, agreement between sources that could not have copied each other is itself evidence. Two stations landing within a millimetre of each other (18 and 19) is the pattern you expect from honest instruments measuring the same weather with small errors. A third value nearly double both is the pattern of a local artefact — a gauge under a dripping roof edge, a blocked funnel cleared mid-storm, a unit slip.

Two disciplines keep triangulation honest. First, independence: three stations repeating one shared upstream feed are really one source wearing three hats, so ask where each number originates before counting votes. Second, do not average the outlier away: (18 + 19 + 34) / 3 ≈ 23.7 mm is a figure no instrument actually supports, and averaging is how a bad measurement contaminates good ones. Report it as 'about 18–19 mm, with one station reporting 34 mm for reasons unknown' — that phrasing preserves both the consensus and the anomaly. If the 34 mm matters, the settling evidence is physical: inspect the gauge, or check radar rainfall estimates for that exact spot.
A software vendor's sales page says 'our support team replies within an hour on average.' I have no way to check that. What would it take to actually verify a claim like that?

Start by recognising the claim's shape: it is not false, it is unverifiable as stated — and naming exactly what evidence would settle it is a verification skill in its own right. Four things are missing. First, the raw material: a timestamped export of support tickets showing when each arrived and when the first human reply was sent. Second, a definition of the average: a mean can hide a long tail — half of tickets answered in five minutes and half in two days also averages near an hour across a bad week, while a median would expose that. Third, the window and exclusions: which months, and whether nights, weekends, and tickets closed without reply were counted or quietly dropped. Fourth, who measured it: the vendor's own dashboard is an interested source; an independent audit or your own trial tickets are not.

Until those exist, the honest status of the claim is 'unsettled', and the practical move is to generate your own evidence: send three test questions at different times of day before signing, and time the replies. Small first-hand samples beat large second-hand assertions. The general rule: for any claim, ask 'what would I look at, and what would it have to show?' If nobody can answer that, the claim is decoration, not information.

A supplier invoice shows: 4 work lamps at $18.50, 2 extension leads at $9.75, 1 ladder at $120.00, subtotal $213.50, tax at 8% shown as $17.08, and a total due of $231.18. Can you verify the whole chain?
Verify each link independently — line items to subtotal, subtotal to tax, tax to total — so a failure is localised to one link:

Two links hold and one fails. Line items recompute to $213.5, matching the stated subtotal. Tax at 8% on $213.50 is $17.08, also matching. But $213.50 + $17.08 = $230.58, while the invoice demands $231.18 — an overcharge of exactly $0.6.

This is why you verify link by link instead of checking only the final total: the failure is now localised to the last addition, and its size is informative. Sixty cents is not a rounding artefact — the tax was already rounded correctly at the previous step — it looks like a stray keying error in the total. Send the invoice back with the chain shown: subtotal agreed, tax agreed, total should be $230.58. Suppliers fix invoices quickly when the discrepancy is demonstrated rather than asserted. And note the asymmetry this exploits: producing a correct invoice requires every link to be right, while verifying one requires only re-walking the chain — checking is cheaper than generating, which is the verifier's permanent advantage.
I'm planning a team lunch with a hard budget cap of $300. My plan: sandwich platters $95, salads $72.50, drinks $64, desserts $45.99, delivery and service $52. Does the plan actually fit the cap?
A plan is verified mechanically against its constraints — sum the plan and compare with the cap, no judgement involved:

The plan fails its constraint: the items total $329.49, which is $29.49 over the $300 cap. Nothing here is a matter of opinion — a budget cap is a mechanical constraint, and the plan as written violates it.

The useful part of a failed check is that it tells you the size of the repair: you must remove at least $29.49 of spend, not 'a bit'. Swapping the $64 drinks package for a $34 one brings the total to $299.49, inside the cap with a small margin. Verifying plans against constraints before execution is the cheapest verification there is, because the cost of the check is one addition while the cost of discovering the violation at the till is real money and embarrassment. The same pattern applies to schedules (do the durations fit the day?), packing (does the weight fit the limit?), and staffing (do the shifts cover the hours?). State the constraint as a number, sum the plan as a number, compare. If they disagree, the plan — not the arithmetic — has to change.
My calculator says 47 x 53 = 2491. I vaguely remember a Victorian trick called casting out nines that checks multiplication without redoing it. Does it work, and does my answer pass?
It works, and here is the mechanism: a number and the sum of its digits leave the same remainder on division by 9, so the remainders must multiply consistently. Checking all three numbers:

Your answer passes. The remainders: 47 leaves 2, 53 leaves 8, and 2 × 8 = 16, which leaves 7 on division by 9. Your product 2491 also leaves 7 — the remainders agree, exactly as they must if the multiplication is right, and the direct product confirms it: 47 × 53 = 2491.

Casting out nines is a checksum in Victorian dress: it compresses each number to a single digit that must satisfy the same arithmetic as the numbers themselves. Its blind spot is instructive — it cannot catch an error that changes the answer by a multiple of 9, which includes the classic digit transposition (2491 vs 2941 differ by 450, a multiple of 9, and both pass). Every checksum has a collision class like this; the craft is knowing which errors your check is blind to and layering a second check that sees them. For transpositions, the mod-11 checks used in book numbers are the stronger net, because their weights make swapped digits change the remainder.

We're tiling a floor in a chessboard pattern, 8 rows of 9 tiles. The tiler says we'll need 37 black tiles and 35 white. Total sounds right (72) but the split feels wrong. Can a split be impossible even when the total is right?

Yes — the total is necessary but not sufficient, and this split is impossible. Work the structure: each row of 9 alternating tiles holds 5 of its starting colour and 4 of the other. Rows alternate which colour they start with, so across 8 rows, four rows start black (5 black, 4 white each) and four start white (4 black, 5 white each). Black tiles: 4 × 5 + 4 × 4 = 36. White tiles: the same, 36. On any rectangular board with an even number of rows, the two colours must come out exactly equal, whatever the row length — so 37/35 cannot tile this floor, even though it sums to the right 72.

This is a parity-style check: instead of recounting the thing itself, you verify a structural property the answer must have. Such checks are everywhere once you look — an odd count claimed for things that come in pairs, a chessboard with two opposite corners removed being 'tileable' by dominoes (it is not; the corners share a colour, and dominoes always cover one of each). When the structure forbids the answer, you do not need to find the tiler's arithmetic slip; the claim refutes itself.

A travel handout lists these conversions: 5 km = 3.11 miles, 70 kg = 154.3 lb, 98.6 F = 37 C, 2 litres = 0.63 US gallons, 60 mph = 96.6 km/h. Present a verification table recomputing each from the standard factors and flag any that fail.

Each conversion recomputed from the standard factors (1 mile = 1.60934 km, 1 kg = 2.20462 lb, 1 US gallon = 3.78541 litres):

| Claim | Recomputed | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 5 km = 3.11 miles | 5 / 1.60934 = 3.11 miles | Pass |
| 70 kg = 154.3 lb | 70 x 2.20462 = 154.3 lb | Pass |
| 98.6 F = 37 C | (98.6 - 32) x 5/9 = 37.0 C | Pass |
| 2 litres = 0.63 US gallons | 2 / 3.78541 = 0.53 gallons | **Fail** — correct value is 0.53 |
| 60 mph = 96.6 km/h | 60 x 1.60934 = 96.6 km/h | Pass |

Four of five pass. The failure is interesting because it is not a rounding slip: 0.63 is roughly what you get using the Imperial gallon (4.546 litres) part-way through a US-gallon calculation — a unit-identity error, the most dangerous kind in conversion tables because the number still looks plausible. Verification tables earn their place exactly here: a handout is a summary of five separate computations, and each one must be re-derived on its own row before the document deserves trust.
A course report states the class average on the midterm was 84. The seven scores were 78, 85, 92, 71, 88, 79, 83. Verify the reported average.
An average is a derived figure — re-derive it from the raw scores, total first, then divide:

The reported average fails verification. The scores total 576, and 576 ÷ 7 = 82.29 — not 84. The report overstates the class average by 1.71 points.

How does an error like this happen? A plausible route: 84 is suspiciously close to the middle score and to the average of the highest and lowest ((92 + 71) / 2 = 81.5, no) — more likely someone averaged a different set, perhaps dropping the 71 or including an eighth score from another section. The verification cannot identify the cause; it establishes the fact and its size. Two-point inflation in a class average is exactly the scale of error that changes grade boundaries and scholarship decisions, yet it survives because almost nobody re-derives a printed average — the number arrives with institutional authority and gets quoted onward. The habit to build: whenever a document hands you a mean and also hands you the data, the data wins. Recompute. It costs thirty seconds and it is the difference between citing a fact and citing a rumour.

My team's shared calendar for Monday lists: standup 9:00-9:15, design review 9:00-10:30, vendor call 10:15-11:00, focus block 11:00-12:30, team lunch 12:30-13:15. The booking tool said everything was fine. Is it?
A calendar is a plan, and plans get verified mechanically: convert times to minutes and test every pair for overlap.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
OVERLAP: standup vs design review — 15 minutes
OVERLAP: design review vs vendor call — 15 minutes
overlaps found

The booking tool was wrong — there are two clashes:

OVERLAP: standup vs design review — 15 minutes
OVERLAP: design review vs vendor call — 15 minutes
overlaps found

The standup (9:00–9:15) sits entirely inside the design review (9:00–10:30), and the vendor call starts at 10:15, fifteen minutes before the design review ends. Note the pairs that pass: the vendor call ending at 11:00 exactly when the focus block begins is fine — touching endpoints are not an overlap, and a good check must know that, or it cries wolf on every back-to-back meeting.

Schedule verification is constraint checking in its most everyday form, and it scales from five meetings to airline timetables: represent each event as an interval, test the pairs, report the size of each violation. The size matters — 'there is a clash' starts an argument; 'the vendor call overlaps the review by 15 minutes' starts a fix, because the repair is exactly 15 minutes of movement. When a tool tells you a plan is fine, remember that the tool usually checked only the bookings it made itself. Your whole day, from every source, is the thing that needs verifying.
Someone is selling a metal bar as solid gold. It measures 10 cm x 5 cm x 2 cm and weighs 1,120 g. Gold's density is 19.3 g per cubic centimetre. Can I check the claim without damaging the bar?
Yes — density is the check, because it is a property the material cannot fake: compute the bar's volume, then its density, and compare with gold's.

The claim fails decisively. The bar's volume is 100 cm³, so its density is 1120 ÷ 100 = 11.2 g/cm³. Solid gold at that volume would weigh 1930 g — this bar is over 800 g light. A density of 11.2 sits nowhere near gold's 19.3; it is in lead's neighbourhood (about 11.3), which suggests a lead core or a lead alloy with a gold-coloured surface.

Density checking is dimensional verification with physical teeth: mass per unit volume, a ratio that stays constant for a pure material at any size, so a measurement anyone can take with a ruler and scales tests a claim about inner composition. It is the same principle as Archimedes in the bath, and customs laboratories still use it as a first screen. Its limits are honest ones: it cannot distinguish gold from tungsten (19.25 g/cm³, nearly identical), which is why serious verification layers a second, independent test — ultrasound or X-ray fluorescence — whose blind spots are different. One check catches most fakes; two checks with different weaknesses catch nearly all.
A shop's newsletter says 'sales rose 25% this year, from $160k to $200k.' Percent claims are wrong so often that I want this one verified properly.
A percent change has a strict definition — change divided by the starting value — and the starting value is where most errors hide. Applying the definition:

This one is correct, verified by two routes. By the definition: the change is $40k, and 40 ÷ 160 = 0.25, so the rise is 25%. By the forward route: growing $160k by 25% gives 160 × 1.25 = $200k, landing exactly on the claimed $200k.

The reason percent claims fail so often is the base. Divide the same $40k change by the ending value instead and you get 20% — the classic error, and the one to check first whenever a percentage smells wrong: ask 'percent of what?' A fall from 200 to 160 described as 'down 25%' would be exactly that error (it is down 20%). The forward-route check used here is the strongest habit of the three: instead of re-deriving the percentage, apply the claimed percentage to the starting figure and see whether you arrive at the claimed ending figure. It converts an abstract ratio back into concrete money, where your intuition can audit it — and it works for interest, discounts, and growth claims alike.

A grant application states that its project summary is exactly 48 words, as the funder requires. The summary reads: 'The committee reviewed the draft proposal on Tuesday and agreed that the budget needed revision before the spring meeting because several line items had grown beyond their original estimates during the winter months and the treasurer was asked to circulate a corrected version to all members before Friday morning for review.' Verify the count.
A stated count is a checksum on a document — verify it by counting the underlying text mechanically rather than by eye:

arguments.code:
text = 'The committee reviewed the draft proposal on Tuesday and agreed that the budget needed revision before the spring meeting because several line items had grown beyond their original estimates during the winter months and the treasurer was asked to circulate a corrected version to all members before Friday morning for review'
words = text.split()
print('actual word count:', len(words))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content: actual word count: 51

The stated count is wrong:

actual word count: 51

The summary actually runs to 51 words, 3 over the funder's limit of 48 — a small discrepancy with non-small consequences if the funder enforces the cap mechanically, as funders increasingly do. The applicant most likely counted an earlier draft and edited without recounting, the document-world equivalent of a stale total in a spreadsheet.

The principle generalises into checksum thinking for documents: any figure a document states about itself — word counts, page counts, totals of its own tables, 'three reasons follow' — is a claim that can be re-derived from the document itself, cheaply and exactly. These self-referential claims fail constantly because editing changes the content while the claim stands still. Before submitting anything with a stated count, recount the final version, not the version you remember. And when you are the reader, a document whose self-counts are wrong is telling you something about the care behind its other, harder-to-check claims.

This two-level check — aggregate matches publication, and total matches the known population — is the template for verifying any reported breakdown: election results against ballots cast, department headcounts against payroll, category sales against the day's takings. When the total is known independently (250 people were in the room), it anchors the whole table; a breakdown can hide a swapped pair of options, but it cannot hide a missing fifty votes. Publish with confidence, and keep the ballot-level data — verification is only ever possible while the underlying records survive.
A store advertises '50% off, then an extra 50% off at the till — that's 100% off, everything free!' My teenager is sceptical. Settle it, and tell me how to think about stacked percentages generally.

Your teenager wins. Percentages stack multiplicatively, not additively, because the second percentage applies to what is left, not to the original price. Take a $200 jacket: the first 50% off leaves $100. The extra 50% off applies to that $100, leaving $50. Total saving: 75%, not 100% — and the extreme-case probe proves it could never be otherwise: if stacking percentages added, two 60% discounts would give 120% off, meaning the shop pays you to take the jacket, which is absurd. A discount can approach 100% but a stack of partial discounts never reaches it.

The general rule: convert each percentage to a multiplier (50% off → ×0.5), multiply the multipliers, and read the result. This is the same mathematics as the percent-change base trap in reverse — percentages are always of something, and in a stack, the 'something' shrinks at every step. It is also why 'up 50% then down 50%' does not bring a price home: ×1.5 then ×0.5 lands at 75% of the start. Whenever percentages are chained — discounts, interest, growth, declines — reach for multipliers, and test any additive claim against the extreme case where it predicts something impossible.

Superlative claims — busiest, largest, most popular, fastest-growing — are the most checkable sentences in any report, because each one is a maximum or minimum over data that usually exists. They are also the claims most often written from impression, because a superlative feels like colour rather than content. The verification habit: whenever a summary names a winner, ask for the full ranking. If the writer cannot produce it, the superlative was never computed, and every decision leaning on it — staffing Tuesdays more heavily, say — is leaning on a guess dressed as a finding.

A recipe from the US says 350 F. I converted to Celsius and got 177, but my oven dial is in Fahrenheit anyway and now I'm second-guessing the formula itself: F to C is (F - 32) x 5/9, right? And is 37 C really 98.6 F?
Verify the formula by round-tripping a value whose answer is independently known — normal body temperature — in both directions:

The formula is right and both directions close. Forward: 37 × 9/5 + 32 = 98.6 °F, the textbook body temperature. Back again with your formula: (98.6 − 32) × 5/9 = 37 °C exactly. A conversion that returns you to your starting point through the inverse operation has verified both the factor and its placement — if the 5/9 and 9/5 were swapped, or the 32 subtracted at the wrong end, the round trip would land somewhere visibly wrong. And your recipe figure checks out too: (350 − 32) × 5/9 ≈ 177 °C.

Round-tripping deserves a permanent place in your toolkit because so many everyday computations have natural inverses: currency conversions, unit conversions, percentage markups and discounts, file compression, encryption. Whenever an inverse exists, applying it to your result and comparing with your input is a complete verification of the arithmetic — though, as always, it certifies the computation, not the input. If the recipe had printed 35O with a letter O, no round trip would save the cake.

Our town council is debating whether the old river bridge is safe. One side quotes a resident who has driven over it for 40 years with no problem. The other side says 'the bridge is unsafe' but hasn't shown anything either. As a resident, what evidence would actually settle this?

Neither side has offered evidence yet — one has an anecdote and the other has an assertion. Forty years of uneventful crossings feels persuasive but is weak evidence about a structure: a bridge can lose half its load capacity to corrosion while still carrying ordinary traffic, because failure is about the worst load on the worst day, not the average of forty years. What would settle the question is specific and exists as a professional discipline. First, the most recent structural inspection report by a licensed bridge engineer — not a summary, the report — with its condition ratings for deck, superstructure, and substructure. Second, the load rating: the maximum weight the bridge is currently certified to carry, compared against the heaviest vehicles that actually cross (school buses, delivery trucks, farm equipment). Third, the inspection interval and any flagged deficiencies with their repair status.

Notice the pattern, because it applies to every 'is it safe / does it work / is it true' dispute: name the quantity that decides the matter (here, rated capacity versus actual loads, and the condition of load-bearing members), identify who measures it competently, and ask for their primary record. Until that record is on the table, the honest position is 'unsettled' — and a council that votes either way before seeing it is voting on rhetoric, not on the bridge.

An employee's timesheet claims: Mon 8h (9:00-17:00, 30 min lunch), Tue 8h (9:00-17:30, 30 min lunch), Wed 7.5h (9:00-16:00, 30 min lunch), Thu 8h (9:00-17:00, 30 min lunch), Fri 6.5h (9:00-16:00, 30 min lunch), total 40h. Present a verification table recomputing each day from the clock times.

Each day recomputed as (clock-out minus clock-in) minus the unpaid lunch:

| Day | Claimed | Recomputed from clock times | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 8h | 9:00-17:00 is 8h, minus 0.5 = 7.5h | **Fail** — overstated by 0.5h |
| Tue | 8h | 9:00-17:30 is 8.5h, minus 0.5 = 8h | Pass |
| Wed | 7.5h | 9:00-16:00 is 7h, minus 0.5 = 6.5h | **Fail** — overstated by 1h |
| Thu | 8h | 9:00-17:00 is 8h, minus 0.5 = 7.5h | **Fail** — overstated by 0.5h |
| Fri | 6.5h | 9:00-16:00 is 7h, minus 0.5 = 6.5h | Pass |
| **Total** | **40h** | **36h** | **Fail** — overstated by 4h |

The table exposes two distinct failures. First, three days are overstated against the clock times: Mon and Thu quietly skip the lunch deduction, and Wed claims 7.5h for a span that holds only 6.5. Second — and this one needs no clock times at all — the claim is internally inconsistent: its own daily figures sum to 38h, not the stated 40h, so the total was wrong before any recomputation began. That layering is typical of real timesheet errors and exactly why verification proceeds in stages: first check the document against itself (do its parts sum to its total?), then check it against the primary record (do the parts match the clock?). Each stage is cheap, each catches errors the other misses, and a document that fails stage one has told you something about the care behind everything else in it.

I need the floor area of an L-shaped room: overall 6 m by 4 m, with a 2 m by 1.5 m notch cut out of one corner. Two flooring calculators gave me different answers (21 and 22.5), so I trust neither. Settle it in a way I can check.
Settle it by computing the area two genuinely different ways — subtract the notch, and build the L from two rectangles — and require the routes to agree:

Both routes agree on 21 m², so the first calculator was right. Route one, subtraction: the full 6 × 4 rectangle is 24 m², minus the 2 × 1.5 notch (3 m²) gives 21 m². Route two, decomposition: slice the L into a 6 × 2.5 strip along the bottom (15 m²) and the remaining 4 × 1.5 block above it (6 m²), totalling 21 m². Two methods that partition the shape differently cannot easily share an error, so their agreement is strong evidence.

The 22.5 figure is diagnosable, too: it is 24 − 1.5, the answer you get if the notch is treated as 1.5 m² instead of 2 × 1.5 = 3 m² — someone multiplied only one of the notch's dimensions. That is the bonus value of a two-route verification: when the routes disagree with a third party's number, the size of the gap often identifies the exact mistake. Order flooring for 21 m² plus your waste allowance — and note the waste allowance is a separate, deliberate addition, not part of the verified area.

Your ledger closes at 3,205; the bank says 3,250; the difference is exactly 45 — and the ledger contains the bank fee twice, at −45 each. One of those entries is a duplicate recording: the bank charged the fee once (its statement is the external record of what actually moved), while your ledger captured it twice, perhaps from both an email alert and the monthly statement import. Remove one fee entry and the ledger closes at exactly 3,250.

Reconciliation works because the two records are produced by different processes with different failure modes, so a disagreement is guaranteed to be informative: its size usually names the culprit, since most errors are a single omitted or duplicated item whose amount equals the gap. When the gap equals no single entry, suspect two errors or a transposition (whose difference is always divisible by 9). Reconcile monthly, while the search space is small — a year's gap can hide a dozen compensating mistakes that net to a deceptively tiny difference.

Our gym issues membership numbers with a mod-11 check digit: digits are weighted 7,6,5,4,3,2,1 from the left and the total must divide by 11. A member insists their number is 7312049 but the system rejects it. Who's right?
The check digit exists precisely to arbitrate this. Running the weighted sum on the number as given, and then computing what the check digit should have been:

arguments.code:
digits = [7,3,1,2,0,4,9]
weights = [7,6,5,4,3,2,1]
total = sum(d*w for d, w in zip(digits, weights))
print('weighted sum:', total)
print('sum mod 11:', total % 11)
print('valid:', total % 11 == 0)
base = sum(d*w for d, w in zip(digits[:6], weights[:6]))
needed = (-base) % 11
print('first six digits weighted sum:', base)
print('correct check digit:', needed)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
weighted sum: 97
sum mod 11: 9
valid: False
first six digits weighted sum: 88
correct check digit: 0

The system is right and the member has misremembered one digit:

weighted sum: 97
sum mod 11: 9
valid: False
first six digits weighted sum: 88
correct check digit: 0

The number as given produces a weighted sum of 97, which leaves 9 on division by 11 — invalid. Working backwards from the first six digits (weighted sum 88, already a multiple of 11), the correct check digit is 0, so the true number is 7312040, not 7312049. A single wrong digit at the end is exactly the failure this scheme was built to catch, and it catches it with certainty: changing any one digit changes the weighted sum by that digit's weight times the change, which cannot be a multiple of 11 for weights 1–7 and digit changes of 1–9.

This is checksum thinking at its most practical. The check digit carries no information about the member — it is pure redundancy, a compressed fingerprint of the other digits, recomputed at every use. Notice the division of labour: the checksum cannot tell you what the right number is in general, but here, because only the final digit was in doubt, the same arithmetic that detected the error also corrects it. Detection is cheap; correction needs either redundancy of this calculable kind or a lookup against the membership database — which is the next step if the member disputes the 0.

Three lab benches measured the same powder sample's mass: 24.6 g, 24.7 g, and 26.9 g. The lab manager wants to report the average, 25.4 g. Is that the right summary, and how would you verify which figure deserves reporting?
Verify the manager's arithmetic first, then test whether the mean is the honest summary by comparing it with the median, which resists a single wild value:

arguments.code:
vals = [24.6, 24.7, 26.9]
mean = sum(vals) / len(vals)
median = sorted(vals)[len(vals) // 2]
print('mean:', round(mean, 2))
print('median:', median)
print('spread of the two agreeing values:', round(24.7 - 24.6, 2))
print('outlier distance from cluster:', round(26.9 - 24.7, 2))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
mean: 25.4
median: 24.7
spread of the two agreeing values: 0.1
outlier distance from cluster: 2.2

The manager's arithmetic is right and the summary is wrong:

mean: 25.4
median: 24.7
spread of the two agreeing values: 0.1
outlier distance from cluster: 2.2

The mean really is 25.4 g — but no bench measured anything near 25.4 g. Two benches agree within 0.1 g of each other, and the third sits 2.2 g away, twenty times the cluster's spread. Averaging folds that suspect value into the report as if it were information; the median, 24.7 g, describes the consensus of the instruments that agree.

The verification principle: when independent measurements cluster, the cluster is the finding and the outlier is a separate investigation. Check the third bench's world before trusting its number — was the sample the same (a different aliquot, a wet sample), was the balance tared with the container, was a digit transposed in the notebook (24.9 read as 26.9, say)? If a cause is found, exclude the value and say why; if none is found, report the cluster and the outlier side by side. What you must not do is let an average silently adjudicate a disagreement between instruments. Averages summarise agreement; they conceal conflict — and concealed conflict in measurements is how bad values get into print wearing good company.

A textbook exercise states: 'A 1000 kg car travelling at 30 m/s has kinetic energy of 30,000 kg m/s.' A student thinks the number and the unit are both suspicious. Check the claim dimensionally and numerically.

The student is right on both counts, and the unit gives the game away before any arithmetic. Kinetic energy is ½mv², so its unit is kg × (m/s)² = kg·m²/s² — the joule. The unit printed, kg·m/s, is mass × velocity: that is momentum's unit, a different quantity wearing energy's name. A dimensional check — does the stated unit match the quantity's formula? — refutes the sentence without touching a calculator.

The number fails too, and instructively: 30,000 is exactly the car's momentum (1000 × 30), which is where the textbook's figure came from — someone computed mv and labelled it ½mv². The actual kinetic energy is ½ × 1000 × 30² = 450,000 joules. Note the two errors are the same error: the formula's square was dropped, which changed both the unit (losing one m/s) and the value (losing a factor of 15). That coupling is why dimensional analysis is such a high-yield check in physics and engineering: a formula mangled in transcription almost always breaks its units, so the units act as a checksum on the algebra. Before computing anything with a formula, derive its unit from the inputs and compare with the unit the answer claims. A mismatch is a certain error; a match is not a guarantee, but it clears the most common failure in one glance.

A student plans this semester: Calculus II (4 credits, needs Calculus I — done last year), Statistics (3 credits, needs Calculus II), Physics (4), Chemistry (3), History (3), Art (2). The college caps a semester at 18 credits. Verify the plan mechanically — credits and prerequisite order.
Both constraints are mechanical, so both can be checked mechanically — total the credits, and test each course's prerequisites against what will actually be completed before it:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content: total credits: 19 | cap: 18 | over by: 1

The plan fails both constraints:

total credits: 19 | cap: 18 | over by: 1

It totals 19 credits against an 18-credit cap, and it schedules Statistics in the same semester as its own prerequisite, Calculus II — a prerequisite is a claim about order, and 'at the same time' does not satisfy 'before'. Either violation alone blocks enrolment; together they mean the plan was assembled by listing wishes rather than by checking rules.

Plan verification generalises directly: extract the constraints as explicit, testable statements (a numeric cap, an ordering, a dependency), then run the plan against every one of them mechanically, because human review of plans fails in a predictable way — we check the constraints we remember and feel the rest. The fix here is also mechanical: drop any 1+ credits to satisfy the cap (Art, at 2 credits, is the natural candidate, which also brings the load to 17), and move Statistics to next semester, when Calculus II will genuinely be in the 'done before' set. A plan that passes its constraints is not guaranteed to be a good plan — but a plan that fails them is guaranteed not to happen as written, and finding that out on paper is the entire point.
Our annual report's headline says 'revenue grew every quarter this year.' The finance table (in $k) shows Q1 210, Q2 235, Q3 228, Q4 260. Verify the headline against the table.
A universal claim ('every quarter') is verified by testing each quarter against its predecessor — one counterexample kills it:

quarter | revenue | change
Q1 | 210 | NULL

Q2 grew by 25 and Q4 by 32, but Q3 fell by 7 (235 → 228). 'Grew every quarter' is false; 'grew in three of four quarters, ending the year up strongly' is what the table supports. Universal claims are the most fragile and the most verifiable kind of summary: 'every', 'always', 'all', 'none' each convert a table into a set of individual tests, and a single failing row refutes the sentence. When you verify a summary, hunt for its universals first — they are where summaries break, because writers reach for them rhetorically ('growth across the board') while the data usually supports only the weaker, truer claim. Note also what did survive verification: revenue did end the year 50k above where it started. The honest headline was available; it was just less sweeping.
A worksheet claims this combustion equation is balanced: C2H6 + 3 O2 -> 2 CO2 + 3 H2O. Verify it the way a chemist would — by counting atoms.
Balancing is a conservation invariant: atoms of each element must be identical on both sides. Counting programmatically so no tally is taken on trust:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
C left: 2 right: 2 balanced
H left: 6 right: 6 balanced
O left: 6 right: 7 MISMATCH

The equation is not balanced:

C left: 2 right: 2 balanced
H left: 6 right: 6 balanced
O left: 6 right: 7 MISMATCH

Carbon and hydrogen tally, but oxygen does not: 6 atoms enter and 7 leave, which is impossible — atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction, so an equation that creates one is wrong regardless of how tidy it looks. The repair: the oxygen coefficient must satisfy 2x = 7, so x = 3.5, or, doubling everything to keep whole numbers, 2 C2H6 + 7 O2 → 4 CO2 + 6 H2O.

Conservation checks are the deepest family of invariants — atoms, mass, charge, energy, money in double-entry books — because they rest on laws rather than conventions. Their verification style is always the same: define the conserved quantity, count it on both sides of the transformation, and refuse any account where the counts differ. The worksheet's error is the classic one: the balancer matched the eye-catching elements (C and H) and stopped one element early. A checklist of what must be conserved, ticked off element by element, is the difference between 'looks balanced' and 'is balanced' — in chemistry and in ledgers alike.

A classmate's quadratic solver claims to 'handle all quadratic equations.' Its code computes the discriminant and takes sqrt of it directly. Which probe inputs would you use to verify that claim, and what do they show?
Verify the universal claim with probes chosen where implementations break: a negative discriminant, a zero leading coefficient, and a double root — plus one ordinary case as a control:

ordinary -> (3.0, 2.0)
negative discriminant -> CRASH: ValueError math domain error
a = 0 (not quadratic) -> CRASH: ZeroDivisionError float division by zero
double root -> (2.0, 2.0)

The claim 'handles all quadratics' fails two of the three probes:

ordinary -> (3.0, 2.0)
negative discriminant -> CRASH: ValueError math domain error
a = 0 (not quadratic) -> CRASH: ZeroDivisionError float division by zero
double root -> (2.0, 2.0)

The ordinary case works (roots 3 and 2) and the double root works (2, 2), but the negative-discriminant case crashes on the square root of −16 — the equation x² + 2x + 5 has perfectly good complex roots (−1 ± 2i) that this solver cannot represent — and a = 0 crashes on division by zero, since the input is not a quadratic at all and the solver never checks.

This is extreme-case probing as a verification method for software: do not test where the code is expected to work; test at the boundaries of its claim, especially where the mathematics changes character (discriminant crossing zero) and where inputs leave the claimed family entirely (a = 0). A claim phrased with 'all' invites exactly this treatment. The repaired claim would be honest and still useful: 'solves quadratics with real roots; reports complex roots as unsupported.' Verification does not just catch bugs — it forces claims to shrink to the size of the evidence, which is where they should have started.

I sent a configuration file to a colleague and want to be sure it arrived byte-identical before she deploys it. The file content is a short text. How does a checksum verify the transfer, and can you demonstrate on the actual content?

Compute a checksum (here CRC32) and the byte count at the source; the receiver computes the same two numbers on what arrived. Any difference in content changes the checksum with overwhelming probability:

arguments.code:
import zlib
sent = b'mode=production
workers=4
timeout_seconds=30
retries=2
'
received = b'mode=production
workers=4
timeout_seconds=30
retries=2
'
print('sent:    ', len(sent), 'bytes, crc32 =', zlib.crc32(sent))
print('received:', len(received), 'bytes, crc32 =', zlib.crc32(received))
print('identical:', sent == received and zlib.crc32(sent) == zlib.crc32(received))
tampered = received.replace(b'workers=4', b'workers=9')
print('if one digit changed: crc32 =', zlib.crc32(tampered), '— same length, different checksum')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
sent:     55 bytes, crc32 = 4223771309
received: 55 bytes, crc32 = 4223771309
identical: True
if one digit changed: crc32 = 3112611760 — same length, different checksum

The demonstration shows both the power and the design of the method:

sent:     55 bytes, crc32 = 4223771309
received: 55 bytes, crc32 = 4223771309
identical: True
if one digit changed: crc32 = 3112611760 — same length, different checksum

The sent and received copies agree on length (55 bytes) and on CRC32, so the transfer is verified. The last line is the important one: changing a single digit keeps the length at 55 bytes but produces a completely different checksum — which is why a checksum is a far stronger check than a byte count alone. Length catches truncation; the checksum catches alteration.

In practice you would have your colleague run the same command on her copy and read you the number, or compare against a checksum published alongside the file. Two honest caveats complete the picture. First, CRC32 is designed to catch accidents, not adversaries — someone deliberately forging a file can also forge its CRC, so for hostile environments you need a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256, whose collisions nobody can manufacture. Second, a matching checksum verifies the file, not its meaning: it proves she has your exact bytes, not that the configuration in them is wise. Verification is layered, and integrity is the layer this check owns.
A course I'm considering buying says 'studies show our study method improves retention by 40%.' There's no citation. What exactly is missing, and what questions would verify or kill this claim?

As stated, the claim is unverifiable — not because it is necessarily false, but because every load-bearing term is undefined. 'Studies' with no citation cannot be located, so start there: which study, published where, by whom, funded by whom? A claim that cannot be traced to a source cannot be checked against it, and untraceable 'studies show' phrasing is itself a finding. Second, 'retention' of what, measured how, after how long? Remembering a word list after ten minutes and remembering course material after a semester are both 'retention', and a method can honestly win the first while losing the second. Third, 'improves by 40%' relative to what — compared with no studying, with rereading, with another active method? And is that 40% relative (from 50% recall to 70%) or 40 percentage points (50% to 90%)? The two readings differ enormously and the sentence is crafted to let you hear the bigger one. Fourth, on whom was it tested, and how many?

The settling evidence would be: the cited paper, its method section, and its results table, checked against each of those questions. Notice that the burden is not symmetric — the seller makes the claim, so the seller supplies the citation; 'you can't prove it doesn't work' is not a defence available to a factual assertion. Until the citation exists, file the claim as marketing, and let the course be judged on things you can verify: a sample lesson, the syllabus, and reviews from identifiable students.

A transcript summary says Maya's GPA is 3.46. Her courses: Biology 4 credits grade 4.0, History 3 credits grade 3.0, Chemistry 3 credits grade 3.7, Art 2 credits grade 2.7. Verify the GPA — and not by the same weighted-average button the summary used.
Route one: the definition, computed directly — total grade points over total credits. Route two: an independent accumulation in code, course by course:

arguments.code:
courses = [('Biology', 4, 4.0), ('History', 3, 3.0), ('Chemistry', 3, 3.7), ('Art', 2, 2.7)]
points = 0.0
credits = 0
for name, cr, g in courses:
    points += cr * g
    credits += cr
    print(name, 'running points:', round(points, 1), 'running credits:', credits)
print('GPA:', round(points / credits, 2))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
Biology running points: 16.0 running credits: 4
History running points: 25.0 running credits: 7
Chemistry running points: 36.1 running credits: 10
Art running points: 41.5 running credits: 12
GPA: 3.46

Both routes land on the transcript's figure. By the definition: grade points are 16 + 9 + 11.1 + 5.4 = 41.5, over 12 credits, giving 41.5 ÷ 12 = 3.46. The independent accumulation agrees step by step:

Biology running points: 16.0 running credits: 4
History running points: 25.0 running credits: 7
Chemistry running points: 36.1 running credits: 10
Art running points: 41.5 running credits: 12
GPA: 3.46

GPA 3.46 verified. The running totals in route two are not decoration — they let you localise any disagreement to a single course, the same reason cross-footing a table beats re-adding a single column.

One subtlety this verification had to respect: a GPA is a weighted mean, and the weights (credits) are part of the claim. The naive check — averaging the four grades, (4.0 + 3.0 + 3.7 + 2.7) / 4 = 3.35 — disagrees with the transcript and would have raised a false alarm. Verifying a derived figure means re-deriving it by its actual definition, weights and all; checking it against a simpler statistic only verifies that the two statistics differ, which you already knew. When a summary and your check disagree, the first suspect is your check's definition, the second is the summary — in that order, every time.
A fund factsheet says: 'The unit price rose 20% in January and fell 20% in February, ending February back where it started the year.' The price on Jan 1 was $250. Verify the claim.
Apply the two changes in sequence, as multipliers, to the actual starting price:

The claim fails. January's rise takes $250 to $300. February's 20% fall applies to $300, not to $250, so it removes $60 and lands at $240 — ten dollars below the start, a net change of -4% over the two months, not zero.

The factsheet's error is the additive fallacy in its most seductive form: equal percentages in opposite directions feel like they cancel, but percentages are fractions of a moving base. The rise is computed on 250, the fall on 300, so the fall is bigger in money. The general repair is the multiplier habit: +20% is ×1.2, −20% is ×0.8, and 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 — any equal up-down pair multiplies to (1 − x²), always below 1. To undo a 20% rise exactly, the fall must be 1 − 1/1.2 = 16.67%, a figure worth remembering whenever a market commentator pairs symmetric percentages. Factsheets are summaries written by interested parties; the two-line recomputation is the reader's entire defence, and it is enough.
Two maps of the same hiking trail disagree: a printed map says 8.5 km, a phone app says 5.6 miles. A trailhead sign says 8.7 km. Which source is the odd one out?
The sources cannot be compared until they share a unit — convert the app figure, then look for the cluster:

Converted, the app's 5.6 miles is 9.01 km. Now the three sources read 8.5, 8.7, and 9.01 km — and the structure is clear: the printed map and the trailhead sign, produced independently, agree within 0.2 km, while the app sits 0.31 km beyond the further of them. The app is the odd one out.

Before demoting it entirely, ask the triangulation question — are the sources measuring the same thing? A plausible reconciliation: the app may route via the service road or include the spur to the viewpoint, measuring a genuinely different path. Disagreement between sources is not always error; sometimes it is a definition wearing a number's clothes, which is why the first move is unit conversion (making comparison possible) and the second is asking what each source actually measured. If all three claim to measure the same trail centreline, then two independent agreements outweigh one dissent, and 8.5–8.7 km is the figure to plan water and daylight around. The app gets reported, not averaged in: splitting the difference to 8.8 would corrupt two good measurements with one bad one.

Present an audit table for a consultant's expense claim. Claimed vs receipt: taxi 38 vs 33, hotel 210 vs 210, meals 64 vs 64, flight 412 vs 412, parking 95 vs 59, supplies 27 vs 27. Recompute the totals, mark each line pass or fail, and state what should be reimbursed.

Every line checked against its receipt — the receipt, not the claim form, is the source document:

| Item | Claimed | Receipt | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Taxi | 38 | 33 | **Fail** — overclaimed by 5 |
| Hotel | 210 | 210 | Pass |
| Meals | 64 | 64 | Pass |
| Flight | 412 | 412 | Pass |
| Parking | 95 | 59 | **Fail** — overclaimed by 36 |
| Supplies | 27 | 27 | Pass |
| **Total** | **846** | **805** | **Overclaimed by 41** |

Reimburse 805, the receipted total. The two failures are different species and an audit table should say so. The taxi gap (5) is the size of a tip added mentally or a fare misremembered — sloppy, common, usually innocent. The parking gap is the fingerprint of a digit transposition: 95 claimed against 59 receipted, the same digits reversed, a difference of 36 — and transposition differences are always divisible by 9, a diagnostic worth keeping (36 ÷ 9 = 4). Neither pattern proves intent, and the audit's job is not to prove intent; it is to establish, line by line, what the evidence supports paying. Four lines pass clean, which matters too: an audit that only reports failures teaches claimants that accuracy is invisible. Record the passes.

Six chess club players held a round-robin (everyone plays everyone once, no draws allowed — games were replayed until decisive). The reported final standings list wins as 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1. A member says the table can't be right. Who's correct, and how can you tell without seeing any game scores?

The member is correct, and the check needs nothing but the tournament's structure. Six players, each pair meeting once, gives 6 × 5 / 2 = 15 games. With no draws, every game produces exactly one win, so the total wins across all players must equal the number of games: 15. The reported standings sum to 16 wins — one more win than there were games to win. At least one player's tally is inflated by one (or a game was counted twice), and the table as printed is impossible.

This is a conservation invariant doing verification work: wins are neither created nor destroyed, merely distributed, so their total is fixed by the format before a single game is played. The same skeleton appears wherever a fixed total is partitioned — votes across candidates cannot exceed ballots cast, hours across projects cannot exceed hours worked, and a league table's total wins must equal its decisive games. The check cannot say whose tally is wrong; for that you go to the game records. But it converts a vague feeling ('the table looks off') into a proof that it is off, by exactly one — and knowing the size of the impossibility tells the secretary precisely how much error to hunt for.

A sauce recipe for 4 uses: tomatoes 400 g, onion 200 g, peppers 100 g, oil 60 g, tomato paste 40 g. I'm scaling to 10 servings and want to verify my scaled quantities (1000, 500, 250, 150, 100) by a completely different route than multiplying each item by 2.5.
The independent route is total mass: scale the whole, then check that the parts sum to it. If both routes agree, the scaling is consistent:

Both routes agree. The base recipe totals 800 g; scaled as a whole by 2.5 it must come to 2000 g. Your itemised quantities sum to 2000 g — the same figure, reached by adding five separately scaled ingredients. Had one item been mis-scaled (the classic slip is scaling the big items and copying a small one unchanged), the parts would have missed the whole by exactly that item's missing growth, and the size of the gap would have named the ingredient.

Total-versus-parts is one of the most portable checks in existence because wholes and parts are computed by different mental operations: the whole by one multiplication, the parts by five. It verifies budgets (line items against the envelope), itineraries (legs against the day), and mixtures (components against the batch weight). Its blind spot is shared assumptions — if the scale factor itself were wrong (you needed 12 servings, not 10), both routes agree on the wrong answer, because both inherit the 2.5. Verification of the factor is a separate, upstream check: 10 servings ÷ 4 servings = 2.5, read straight off the problem. Check the inputs, then check the arithmetic — in that order.
