And when the numbers disagree, do not just note the gap: divide it by the quantities in the table. Discrepancies that factor neatly against a row are confessions about which row, and which field, went wrong.

A loan calculator says my $12,000 loan at 12% APR over 12 monthly payments costs $1,066.19 a month, with $120 of the first payment being interest. Verify both figures — and is there an extreme case that checks the interest logic on its own?

Verify the interest figure by definition first (one month of interest on the full balance), then the payment by the amortisation formula, then probe the formula at a one-month term where the answer is known by pure reasoning:

Both figures verify. First month's interest is by definition the balance times the monthly rate: 12,000 × 0.12 ÷ 12 = $120 — matches. The payment formula gives $1066.19 — matches. And the extreme probe confirms the formula's logic: at a one-month term it returns $12120, which is exactly the principal plus one month's interest (12,000 + 120), the only answer a one-month loan can have. A formula that is right at the boundary and right at the definition earns trust in the middle. As a bonus, the split of the first payment follows: $1066.19 − $120 = $946.19 goes to principal, which is why early payments barely dent the balance.

Notice the verification strategy, because it transfers to any black-box calculator: check one component by its definition, check the composite by an independent formula, and probe an extreme case where the correct output is forced by reasoning alone. Three cheap tests, three different failure modes covered. What remains unverified is the inputs — that 12% is really the APR and not a flat rate in disguise is a question for the loan documents, not for arithmetic.

Payment forms reject mistyped card numbers instantly, before any bank is contacted. The number 4539 1488 0343 6467 passes, but changing the last digit to 8 fails. What check is the form running? Demonstrate it on both versions.
The form runs the Luhn checksum: double every second digit from the right, subtract 9 from any doubled value over 9, sum everything — the total must divide by 10. Running it on both versions:

The checksum explains the form's behaviour exactly:

4539148803436467 -> sum 80 -> valid
4539148803436468 -> sum 81 -> INVALID

The genuine number's digits, after the doubling dance, sum to 80 — divisible by 10, so it passes. Changing only the final digit raises the sum to 81, and the check fails before any network call is made. That final digit is a check digit: it was chosen by the card issuer precisely to make the total land on a multiple of 10, so the number carries its own verification wherever it goes.

Luhn's design targets the errors humans actually make: it catches every single-digit typo, and nearly every transposition of adjacent digits (the one blind pair is 09 ↔ 90, a known and accepted weakness). It is vital to be clear about what it does not do: a Luhn-valid number is merely well-formed, not real, not funded, not the typist's own. The form's instant rejection is a format check, and the bank's later approval is an entirely separate verification. Confusing the two — 'the site accepted my number, so the payment is fine' — is a category error that checksum literacy prevents.
A charity's annual letter says 'our membership has doubled since 2019, from 41,000 to 79,000 members.' Verify the word 'doubled'.
'Doubled' is a precise claim — a ratio of exactly 2 — so verify it as a ratio, and also compute what doubling would have required:

The claim fails, though the underlying growth is real. The ratio is 1.927 — membership grew by 92.7%, which is substantial, but doubling requires 82000 members, and the charity is 3000 short of that line.

Why does this matter enough to check? Because 'doubled' is not a loose synonym for 'grew a lot' — it is a multiplier, and multipliers are checkable claims that readers repeat. A journalist quoting the letter writes 'membership doubled', a donor hears momentum that is 3,000 members stronger than reality, and the exaggeration compounds with each retelling. The verification cost was one division. Note the shape of the near-miss: 79 is close to 82, and numbers that fall just short of a round claim are where exaggeration lives — nobody writes 'doubled' about a rise from 41 to 55. The habit to build: whenever prose attaches a multiplier word (doubled, tripled, halved, tenfold) to two numbers, divide the numbers. The word must match the ratio, or the word — not the growth — gets corrected.

My itinerary: flight one lands in Denver at 11:40 local, my connection departs 12:15 local from the same airport. The booking site calls this a 'valid connection' and the airline's own minimum connection time is 45 minutes. Verify the itinerary against the constraint.
A connection is an interval between two clock times — verify it by computing the interval and comparing it with the stated minimum, in the same timezone throughout:

arguments.code:
from datetime import datetime
fmt = '%H:%M'
arrive = datetime.strptime('11:40', fmt)
depart = datetime.strptime('12:15', fmt)
gap = (depart - arrive).seconds // 60
print('connection time:', gap, 'minutes')
print('minimum required: 45 minutes')
print('verdict:', 'OK' if gap >= 45 else f'TOO TIGHT by {45 - gap} minutes')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
connection time: 35 minutes
minimum required: 45 minutes
verdict: TOO TIGHT by 10 minutes

The itinerary fails its own airline's constraint:

connection time: 35 minutes
minimum required: 45 minutes
verdict: TOO TIGHT by 10 minutes

Thirty-five minutes is not forty-five, and no amount of 'valid connection' labelling from the booking site changes the arithmetic — the site's label likely reflects a different, looser rule (or a codeshare partner's minimum), which is precisely why you verify against the constraint that governs your ticket, not the one that governed the sale.

Two features make this check worth doing carefully. First, everything was converted to one timezone before subtracting — the single most common itinerary error is subtracting times that live in different zones, which manufactures phantom hours. Second, the verdict names the size of the violation: 10 minutes short. That number is the negotiation — a 10-minute shortfall on a 45-minute rule is a rebooking conversation, while a 3-hour shortfall would be a different trip. Mechanical constraint checks like this one (intervals versus minimums, totals versus caps, dates versus deadlines) share a virtue: they are entirely decidable from the documents in front of you. No expertise, no judgement, no trust in the seller required.
A hosting provider advertises '99.9% uptime, guaranteed.' Before I move my shop's site there, what would verify that claim, and what does 99.9% actually permit them?

First, translate the percentage into time, because percentages hide scale: 99.9% uptime permits 0.1% downtime, which over a 30-day month is 43.2 minutes, and over a year about 8.8 hours. Whether that is acceptable depends on when those minutes land — 43 minutes at 3 a.m. is a footnote; 43 minutes across a Saturday sale is a disaster — and the claim is silent on distribution, which is the first thing to notice.

What would verify it: the provider's own status page history is a start but is self-graded homework, so weight it lightly. Stronger evidence is an independent monitoring record — third-party uptime services publish histories for major hosts — plus the SLA document itself, read for definitions: does 'uptime' exclude scheduled maintenance (it usually does, sometimes generously), is it measured monthly or yearly, per-server or across the network, and what is the remedy — a guarantee whose only remedy is a small service credit is a marketing statement wearing a contract's clothes. Finally, your own evidence beats all of it after the fact: run a free external monitor from day one, pinging every five minutes, so that at renewal time you hold your own log rather than their summary. The pattern is the same as every unverifiable-claim check: convert the claim into observable quantities, find who measures them without an interest in the answer, and where nobody does, become the measurer.

In a training exercise for vet techs: a medication is dosed at 5 mg per kg. The patient weighs 70 kg. The stock solution is 50 mg per mL. A trainee calculated the dose as 350 mg (correct so far) but then said to draw up 0.7 mL. Verify the volume, dimensionally.
The trainee's dose in milligrams is right; the volume is where the check belongs. Volume must come from dose divided by concentration — and the units will confirm the direction:

The trainee's volume is wrong by a factor of ten, and the unit check exposes exactly how. The dose is 5 mg/kg × 70 kg = 350 mg (the kg cancel — the signature of a correct setup). Volume = dose ÷ concentration: 350 mg ÷ 50 mg/mL, the mg cancel and mL survives, giving 7 mL. The trainee instead divided the numbers the wrong way at the last step (or divided 35 by 50), landing on 0.7 mL — a tenth of the intended dose. The wrong-direction multiplication, 17500, would carry units of mg²/mL, a unit that means nothing, which is the tell: whenever a computation's units come out meaningless, the operation was inverted somewhere.

Dimensional verification is the professional's first line of defence in any dosed, rated, or converted quantity, because it is independent of the numbers: you can check the shape of the calculation with the values covered up. In clinical and engineering settings the habit is ritualised — write every quantity with its unit, cancel explicitly, and refuse any result whose unit is not the unit you set out to produce. A factor-of-ten error is the most dangerous arithmetic slip in dosage work, and it is precisely the kind a unit check catches before anything is drawn up.

Build a verification matrix for a fictional product page selling a lantern. Claims: '20-hour battery life', 'IP68 waterproof', 'ships within 24 hours', 'over 10,000 sold', '2-year warranty'. Evidence on file: lab test measured 17.5 hours at full brightness; the IP68 certificate from the testing lab is on file; warehouse logs show a median dispatch time of 31 hours last month; the sales ledger counts 9,412 units; the warranty terms document states 2 years. Mark each claim verified or failed with the deciding evidence.

Each claim tested against the strongest evidence on file — not against the product page's own assertions:

| Claim | Evidence checked | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 20-hour battery life | Lab test at full brightness: 17.5 hours | **Fail** — overstated by 2.5 hours (a lower brightness setting might reach 20, but the claim does not say that) |
| IP68 waterproof | Testing lab's IP68 certificate on file | Verified — third-party document, matches the claim exactly |
| Ships within 24 hours | Warehouse logs: median dispatch 31 hours last month | **Fail** — the typical order misses the promise by 7 hours; a median is the right statistic here, since half of all orders wait longer |
| Over 10,000 sold | Sales ledger count: 9,412 units | **Fail** — short by 588; 'over 10,000' is a threshold claim and 9,412 does not cross it |
| 2-year warranty | Warranty terms document: 2 years | Verified — primary document, matches |

Two verified, three failed — and the pattern of the failures is the lesson of the matrix format. Every failed claim is a number that drifted from its source: a lab result rounded up into a headline, a dispatch target quoted as a dispatch record, a sales count rounded to the nearest boast. Every verified claim is one whose evidence is a document produced by somebody else (a lab, a terms sheet) for a purpose other than selling. A verification matrix forces this claim-by-claim honesty: no overall impression of 'mostly accurate', no averaging of truth. A page is not 60% trustworthy; it is five separate claims, two of which you may rely on and three of which you may not — and now you know which.

A project review lists the possible outcomes for a launch and their probabilities: success 0.42, partial success 0.31, failure 0.24, and states 'these are all the outcomes we consider possible.' Check that statement.
If the list is truly exhaustive and the outcomes cannot overlap, the probabilities must sum to exactly 1. Testing the invariant:

The statement fails: the probabilities sum to 0.97, leaving 0.03 of probability mass unaccounted for. Three percent of the future is missing from the review. Either an outcome was dropped from the list (the classic candidate: 'delayed launch', quietly folded into nothing), or one of the three figures was rounded or mistyped downward.

A missing 0.03 is not pedantry. Decisions are made on these numbers — an expected-value calculation run on this table silently treats the missing outcomes as impossible, and if the missing mass is a bad outcome (delay, cancellation), every risk figure downstream is understated. The invariant check cannot tell you which outcome is missing; it tells you the list is incomplete and by how much, which converts a vague review into a pointed question: 'what has a 3% chance that we are not discussing?' Probability tables in risk registers, forecasts, and models deserve this five-second audit every time, because the rows that vanish from such tables are disproportionately the inconvenient ones.
A market trader did this multiplication by hand and wrote 38 x 24 = 892. Use casting out nines to check it before I pay the invoice based on it.
Casting out nines: compare the digit-root of the claimed product with the product of the digit-roots of the factors. They must match:

Do not pay on that figure — the check catches the error. The factors leave remainders 2 and 6; 2 × 6 = 12, which casts to 3. So the true product must leave remainder 3 on division by 9. The claimed 892 leaves 1. Mismatch: the trader's answer is certainly wrong. The actual product is 912 — and 912 duly leaves remainder 3, as it must.

Study the division of labour in this check, because it is the template for all checksum verification. The check is one-directional: a mismatch proves error, but a match would only have been consistent with correctness, not proof of it (any wrong answer differing by a multiple of 9, like 921, slips through). That asymmetry is not a defect to apologise for — it is the economics of verification. A near-free test that catches most errors, run first, reserves expensive full recomputation for the cases that survive. The trader was out by 20, a plausible slip of hand arithmetic; the invoice should be reissued at 912 units' value, and the episode is a tidy argument for checksums on every hand-computed figure that money follows.

The minutes summarise the transcript, so verify the summary against the source by counting the markers mechanically rather than re-reading prose:

The transcript records four decisions; the minutes report three. Anyone acting from the minutes alone will miss a commitment the meeting actually made.

This is the summary-versus-source check in its documentary form, and it generalises to every 'the report says N' situation: counts of decisions, action items, defects, signatories. The mechanical count matters because prose summaries are written by humans summarising from memory and emphasis, while markers in the source are created at the moment of the event. Where a source has explicit markers, count the markers; where it does not, the honest finding is that the summary is unverifiable from the text alone and must be checked against recordings or attendees. Note, too, the asymmetry of the error's direction: summaries almost always undercount commitments and overcount achievements. Knowing which way a genre of document tends to drift tells you which claims in it to verify first.

A contractor says his pump, rated at 45 litres per minute, ran for 2.5 hours and filled our 8,000-litre tank from empty to full. The tank gauge now reads full. Verify his account before I sign off the invoice.
Verify the delivered volume independently of the gauge: rate multiplied by time, with the units tracked:

The contractor's account does not add up. In 150 minutes at 45 L/min, the pump delivers 6750 litres — 1250 litres short of the tank's 8,000. To deliver 8,000 litres at that rate takes 177.8 minutes, about 2 hours 58 minutes, not 2 hours 30. Either the pump ran longer than invoiced (good news for him, if he amends it), the pump's true rate exceeds its rating, or the tank was not empty at the start — the gauge reading 'full' is consistent with all three, which is why the gauge alone settles nothing.

Rate × time = volume is a dimensional identity, and claims built on it are fully checkable from the claimant's own numbers: no site visit, no instruments, just the multiplication the invoice itself invites. The shortfall here is about 16% of the claimed volume — far outside any rounding defence. Sign nothing until the discrepancy is explained in one of the three ways above, each of which is itself verifiable (run-time logs, a measured flow test, the previous gauge reading). Verification rarely ends with 'wrong'; it ends with a short list of specific worlds in which the numbers could be right, and a request to show we live in one of them.

A student wrote a palindrome checker that compares first and last characters and recurses inward, with no base case for short strings. They tested it on 'ab', got False (correct), and concluded it works. Verify it properly — what probes expose it?
Probe the inputs the student never tried: actual palindromes, a single character, and the empty string — the places where a recursion without a base case must eventually arrive:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
'racecar' -> CRASH: IndexError
'noon' -> CRASH: IndexError
'ab' -> False
'a' -> CRASH: IndexError
'' -> CRASH: IndexError

The probes demolish the conclusion:

'racecar' -> CRASH: IndexError
'noon' -> CRASH: IndexError
'ab' -> False
'a' -> CRASH: IndexError
'' -> CRASH: IndexError

Only 'ab' — the student's single test — returns at all, and it returns by the mismatch exit, the one path that never recurses. Every palindrome crashes: 'racecar' and 'noon' recurse inward, matching pair by pair, until the string is empty and s[0] indexes a character that does not exist. A single character crashes the same way, and so does the empty string. The function does not merely have an edge-case bug; it cannot successfully recognise any palindrome at all. The student's verification failed because their one test exercised the only branch that works — a False result for a non-palindrome — and they generalised from it.

This is the central lesson of probe selection: a test that cannot fail teaches nothing. The student's test was guaranteed to pass by the code's structure, like checking a smoke alarm by confirming it is quiet. Verification probes must be chosen where failure is possible and informative — here, inputs that force the recursion to its missing base case. The fix is two lines (return True when len(s) <= 1, since a string of length 0 or 1 is trivially a palindrome), after which the same probe set passes in full. Choose probes at the boundaries of the claim, especially the boundaries the author avoided, and let the claim earn its confidence there.

Three polls for the same local election, all this week: Poll A has Candidate Rios ahead by 4 points, Poll B has Rios ahead by 1, Poll C has her opponent ahead by 2. Each poll reports a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 points. The campaigns are each quoting the poll they like. As a voter, how do I verify what these polls actually establish?

Start by converting each headline into the interval it actually claims. A lead of 4 with a ±3.5 margin means Rios's true lead is plausibly anywhere from +0.5 to +7.5. Poll B's +1 means anything from −2.5 to +4.5. Poll C's −2 means anything from −5.5 to +1.5. Now lay the three intervals over each other: they share a common region, roughly +0.5 to +1.5 — a small Rios lead is consistent with all three polls simultaneously. That overlap is the triangulation: three independent measurements, each imprecise, jointly support a narrower conclusion than any headline — the race is close, with Rios probably fractionally ahead, and a tie or a small deficit not excluded.

Two verification disciplines matter here. First, independence: if the three polls share a likely-voter model or one copied another's weighting, their agreement is worth less — check the pollsters and methods, not just the numbers. Second, refuse the campaigns' framing: quoting the favourable poll is not lying about that poll, it is lying about the set. The set is the evidence. When sources disagree within their stated uncertainties, the honest report is the overlap and the spread, not a winner. A voter who reads polls this way is doing real verification: not 'which number is right?' but 'what is the strongest statement all the evidence can carry together?' — usually less dramatic, and actually true.

Payroll is where verification stops being an intellectual exercise — an underpayment is a legal liability and a person's rent. Note the method's economy: the recomputation needed nothing but the hours and rates already on the payslip, and the diagnosis came free from the structure of the difference. A discrepancy that factors neatly (here, into hours × premium) is a signature of the exact line that failed. Pay Ben the $45, then check whether the same template error touched other employees' overtime — a systematic template bug rarely strikes once, and finding it in one payslip obliges you to look at them all.
I encrypted a note with a Caesar shift of 7 and got 'TLLA HA UVVU'. Before I send it, verify the encryption is sound — that it can be decrypted back to the original 'MEET AT NOON' with no loss.
An encryption scheme verifies by round trip: encrypt the plaintext, decrypt the ciphertext with the inverse shift, and require the original back, character for character:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
plaintext : MEET AT NOON
encrypted : TLLA HA UVVU
decrypted : MEET AT NOON
round trip exact: True

The round trip closes exactly:

plaintext : MEET AT NOON
encrypted : TLLA HA UVVU
decrypted : MEET AT NOON
round trip exact: True

Encrypting 'MEET AT NOON' with shift 7 reproduces your ciphertext 'TLLA HA UVVU', and shifting back by 7 restores the plaintext character for character, spaces intact. The scheme is lossless for this message — whatever your correspondent does with the inverse shift, they will read exactly what you wrote.

Round-trip verification is the right test for any reversible transformation — encryption, compression, encoding, unit conversion, file format migration — because the property you care about is precisely that the inverse exists and is exact. Its scope deserves the usual care: this verifies fidelity, not secrecy. A Caesar cipher is transparent to anyone who tries 25 shifts, so the note is verified as recoverable, not as private. Keeping those two verdicts separate — 'the transformation is faithful' versus 'the transformation is safe' — is the whole of verification discipline in miniature: each check certifies one property, and no check certifies properties it did not test.

I'm about to publish a quarterly report. Give me a pre-flight verification checklist as a table — the checks I should run, what each one catches, and how to run it — based on the state of my draft: totals cross-footed yesterday, percentage shares not yet summed, one chart has no axis units, and a figure on page 3 is labelled with last year's date.

Pre-flight checks for the draft, ordered cheapest first — each row is a check, the failure it hunts, and its current status in your draft:

| # | Check | How to run it | Catches | Status in your draft |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Parts sum to totals | Add every breakdown; compare with its stated total | Dropped rows, stale totals | Done yesterday — re-run if any figure changed since |
| 2 | Percentage shares sum to 100 | Add every set of shares of one whole | Over-promising splits, missing categories | **Not yet run — do this next** |
| 3 | Every chart carries units | Read each axis and label aloud | Unit mix-ups invisible in the numbers | **Fail — one chart has no axis units; add them** |
| 4 | Dates and periods consistent | Search the document for the year; check every figure's period label | Last year's figure in this year's report | **Fail — page 3 figure carries last year's date; correct or remove** |
| 5 | Superlatives backed by rankings | For every 'largest/first/most', produce the full ranking | Impressions dressed as findings | Not yet checked |
| 6 | Derived figures re-derived | Recompute each average, ratio, and growth rate from the raw data | Wrong-base percentages, stale spreadsheets | Not yet checked |
| 7 | Cross-references resolve | Follow every 'see page X / table Y' | Renumbering drift after edits | Not yet checked |

The checklist's logic is layered verification: internal consistency first (rows 1–2, which need no outside data), then labelling integrity (3–4), then the claims themselves (5–6), then the document's plumbing (7). Two of your four known items are already failures — fix those before running the rest, because a document with wrong dates and missing units has announced the level of care in its preparation, and the deeper checks in rows 5 and 6 deserve extra suspicion, not less. Publish only when every row reads pass; a checklist with a known fail left in is not a checklist, it is a confession.

I mix 3 kg of a 20% salt solution with 2 kg of a 10% salt solution. A colleague says the result is 15% 'because that's the average of 20 and 10.' Verify the true concentration using conservation of mass.
Salt is conserved: track the salt itself, not the percentages. Total salt in must equal total salt out, and the concentration is salt over total mass:

Your colleague's 15% fails the mass balance. The first solution carries 3 × 0.20 = 0.6 kg of salt; the second carries 2 × 0.10 = 0.2 kg. Total salt: 0.8 kg, dissolved in 5 kg of mixture, so the concentration is 0.8 ÷ 5 = 16% — not 15%.

The colleague's error is averaging percentages as if they were plain numbers. Percentages are ratios with denominators, and here the denominators differ: the 20% describes 3 kg, the 10% describes 2 kg, so the stronger solution rightly pulls the result above the midpoint. The correct average is weighted by mass — and mass balance gives it to you without any formula for weighted averages, just bookkeeping on a conserved quantity. This is the deepest pattern in this whole family of checks: when percentages, rates, or averages mislead, drop down one level to the conserved stuff underneath — salt, money, votes, hours — total that, and rebuild the ratio at the end. Ratios of totals are trustworthy; averages of ratios are where errors breed.
A dashboard for weekly delivery times (days) reports 'median delivery time: 24.9'. The raw values for the period are 12, 15, 14, 90, 13, 16, 14. That median looks wrong to me. Verify it.
A median is a positional statistic — verify it by sorting the data and taking the middle value, and also compute the mean to see whether the dashboard confused the two:

s = sorted(vals)
median = s[len(s) // 2]
mean = sum(vals) / len(vals)
print('sorted:', s)
print('median (middle value):', median)
print('mean:', round(mean, 1))

mean: 24.9

Your suspicion is right — the dashboard's 'median' is the mean wearing the wrong label:

sorted: [12, 13, 14, 14, 15, 16, 90]
median (middle value): 14
mean: 24.9

Sorted, the middle value is 14 days. The figure 24.9 is the mean, dragged upward by the single 90-day outlier. The two statistics tell opposite stories about this data: the median says a typical delivery takes a fortnight; the mean says three and a half weeks, a value no actual delivery came near except the disaster at 90.

Mislabeled statistics are a distinct verification target because the arithmetic can be perfect while the label lies. The defence is definitional: for any reported statistic, state its definition in one sentence ('the value half the deliveries beat') and test the figure against that sentence on the raw data. Medians and means diverge exactly when data is skewed, which is exactly when the choice between them matters — with one 90 in a set of fortnight-ish values, reporting the mean as the median overstates typical delivery time by 78%. When a dashboard gives you a statistic and the raw values, recompute both candidates; the one that matches tells you what the pipeline actually calculates, whatever its label claims.

A supplement advert says 'clinically proven to boost focus.' No study is named. What would it take to verify this, and what are the tells that the phrase is doing marketing work rather than reporting evidence?

Treat 'clinically proven' as a claim with four missing coordinates, each of which is a question the advertiser should be able to answer. Which clinic, which trial: a real clinical claim points to a registered trial or a published paper with authors, a journal, and a date — ask for the citation, and check whether it exists and whether it studied this product (not merely an ingredient in it, at a different dose, in a different population). Proven to do what, measured how: 'focus' must be an operational measure — a named attention test, a reaction-time task — not a mood questionnaire the subjects filled in about themselves. Proven against what: a trial without a placebo control cannot separate the supplement from the expectation of benefit, which for focus is large. And proven how strongly, in how many people: an effect in 14 volunteers for one afternoon is a pilot, not a proof.

The tells that the phrase is decoration: no citation anywhere on the page or packaging; the claim attaches to the product while the fine print cites an ingredient; asterisks leading to 'these statements have not been evaluated' disclaimers, which legally retract in small print what the headline asserts in large. The settling evidence is specific and either exists or does not: a trial registration number you can look up. Until it is produced, the verified statement is not 'the supplement does not work' — it is 'no public evidence has been offered that it does', and a claim with no offered evidence should be priced accordingly: at zero.

A health app reports my BMI as 26.8 from 85 kg and 1.78 m. I want to verify it by a completely different route — the imperial formula with pounds and inches (703 x lb / in^2). 85 kg is 187.39 lb and 1.78 m is 70.08 in. Do the routes agree?
Compute both routes from their own inputs and compare — agreement between unit systems is a strong cross-check because the formulas share no arithmetic:

The routes agree to within a hundredth: metric gives 26.83, imperial gives 26.82. The app's 26.8 is the honest rounding of both. The residual 0.01 is not an error in either formula — it is the rounding you introduced when converting the inputs (187.39 lb and 70.08 in are themselves rounded), and it shows up in the last digit exactly where rounding residue belongs.

Cross-system verification is unusually strong because the two computations share nothing but the underlying person: different numbers, different constants (the 703 is itself a bundle of conversion factors), different arithmetic paths. An error in the app — a transposed height, a pounds/kilograms mix-up — would have to produce the same wrong answer through both systems to survive, and unit mix-ups in particular cannot survive, because the imperial route would expose a metric input instantly (85 'pounds' would give a BMI near 12). When two routes agree only approximately, judge the gap against the precision of the inputs: a hundredth here, from inputs rounded to a hundredth, is agreement. A gap of a whole point would be a finding.

A merged report PDF has 59 pages. Its sections are: introduction 4 pages, chapter 1 — 18, chapter 2 — 22, chapter 3 — 15, and an appendix of 12 pages that the table of contents lists. Verify the merged document is complete.
A document's completeness is a sum: the parts must total the whole. Adding the sections both with and without the appendix:

The merged document is incomplete, and the arithmetic names the missing piece exactly. The body sections total 59 pages — precisely the PDF's 59. With the appendix, the report should run to 71 pages. The gap is 12 pages, which is the appendix's exact length: the appendix was never merged in, even though the table of contents still promises it.

Page-count reconciliation is the document form of the completeness check, and it catches the most common assembly error in reports, filings, and contracts — a section dropped during merging, scanning, or export, while the contents page (written earlier, from intention rather than from the final file) continues to list it. The diagnostic elegance is in the gap's size: a shortfall equal to one whole section means a missing section; a shortfall of one or two pages means lost leaves within a section, a different hunt entirely. Whenever a document states its own extent — pages, words, line items, attachments — recount from the parts before relying on it. Documents, like invoices, should be verified at the seams where they were assembled.

This is why double-entry's invariant is tested at multiple levels. A whole-journal imbalance tells you an error exists and its size; the same invariant applied per transaction tells you where. The size was already a clue — 270 is not divisible by 9, ruling out the classic digit transposition, and it matches no single legitimate entry, ruling out a simple omission. Structured invariants turn error-hunting from reading everything into bisecting: test the whole, then halves, then quarters, until the failing region is one entry wide. Bookkeepers did this by hand for centuries; the query merely makes explicit what their method always was.

A colleague 'optimised' our sorting routine by converting the list to a set first, then sorting. Their tests pass: the output is always in order. I say sortedness is not the only property a sort must preserve. Demonstrate the full verification.
A correct sort must satisfy two invariants: the output is ordered, and the output is a permutation of the input — same elements, same multiplicities. Testing both on a list with repeated values:

from collections import Counter
def fast_sort(xs):
    return sorted(set(xs))
data = [4, 1, 7, 1, 9, 4, 4, 2]
out = fast_sort(data)
print('input :', data, 'len', len(data))
print('output:', out, 'len', len(out))
print('invariant 1 — ordered:', all(out[i] <= out[i+1] for i in range(len(out)-1)))
print('invariant 2 — same multiset:', Counter(out) == Counter(data))
print('lost elements:', list((Counter(data) - Counter(out)).elements()))

output: [1, 2, 4, 7, 9] len 5
invariant 1 — ordered: True
invariant 2 — same multiset: False
lost elements: [4, 4, 1]

Your colleague's tests pass and their sort is broken — both, because their tests only check one of the two invariants:

output: [1, 2, 4, 7, 9] len 5
invariant 1 — ordered: True
invariant 2 — same multiset: False
lost elements: [4, 4, 1]

The output is perfectly ordered, so invariant 1 holds. But invariant 2 fails: eight elements went in, five came out. The set conversion silently deleted the duplicate 1s and two of the three 4s. Any downstream count, sum, or average computed on the 'sorted' data is now wrong, while looking impeccably organised.

The general lesson is that verifying a transformation means enumerating the properties it must preserve and testing each one — sortedness and permutation for sorts; totals and row counts for data migrations; mass and charge for chemical equations. Bugs live in the properties nobody listed. A useful discipline when reviewing any 'optimisation': ask what the original code guaranteed, in writing, and make the new code pass tests for every guarantee, not just the headline one. The colleague's routine is a fine deduplicator; it was verified as the wrong thing. Verification begins by stating, completely, what 'correct' means — most failures are born there, not in the code.

A report on eight sampled measurements (22, 27, 31, 29, 35, 41, 38, 33) states 'sample standard deviation: 5.7'. A reviewer recomputed and got 6.1. One of them used the wrong formula. Verify from the raw data and identify exactly what happened.
Recompute both candidate statistics from the raw values — the population formula (divide by n) and the sample formula (divide by n−1) — and see which claim each matches:

import math
data = [22, 27, 31, 29, 35, 41, 38, 33]
n = len(data)
mean = sum(data) / n
ss = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in data)
print('mean:', mean)
print('sum of squared deviations:', ss)
print('population SD (divide by n):', round(math.sqrt(ss / n), 2))
print('sample SD (divide by n-1):', round(math.sqrt(ss / (n - 1)), 2))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
mean: 32.0
sum of squared deviations: 262.0
population SD (divide by n): 5.72
sample SD (divide by n-1): 6.12

Both people computed correctly — from different definitions:

mean: 32.0
sum of squared deviations: 262.0
population SD (divide by n): 5.72
sample SD (divide by n-1): 6.12

The report's 5.7 is the population standard deviation; the reviewer's 6.1 is the sample standard deviation. The report's number is wrong for its own label: the data are a sample (eight measurements drawn to characterise a larger process), so the sample formula with n−1 applies, and the stated figure understates the spread by about 7%.

This is a verification case where recomputation alone does not settle the matter — you must verify the definition, not just the arithmetic. The n−1 (Bessel's correction) exists because a sample's deviations are measured from the sample's own mean, which sits closer to the data than the true mean does, systematically shrinking the spread; dividing by n−1 compensates. The practical habits: whenever a summary statistic is quoted, ask which variant it is (population or sample SD, mean or median, gross or net); and when you recompute, compute the plausible variants and see which one the claim matches — a claim that matches a different definition than its label is a labelling error, the most respectable and most common kind of statistical error in print.

Our town's founding year is given as 1839 on a plaque in the square, 1847 in a newspaper centennial article, and 1852 in a county history book. The council wants one date for a new sign. How do I verify which, if any, is right — the sources just contradict each other.

Contradiction between sources is the beginning of verification, not the end — the work is to grade the sources and check their independence. Start with genealogy: sources that copy each other count once. The newspaper's centennial article is suspicious on its face — a centennial piece is written backwards from an anniversary, so if the town celebrated a centennial in 1947, the article's 1847 may be derived from the celebration rather than from records; worse, the celebration's date may itself trace to the plaque. The county history (1852) sounds weightier, but county histories were often compiled from subscriber submissions and earlier local pamphlets — ask what it cites. The plaque (1839) is a physical artefact, but plaques commemorate; they do not document, and this one was presumably cast long after any of the candidate dates.

What would settle it is a primary record created at the time for a purpose other than commemoration: the town's incorporation filing or first council minutes, a land-office plat, a post office establishment record, a contemporary newspaper issue. One such document outweighs all three secondary sources, because verification weights evidence by proximity to the event and by independence from the claim. If the primary record shows, say, incorporation in 1852 with settlement from 1839, then all three sources were answering different questions — first settler, first celebration, legal founding — and the council's real task is choosing which event the sign should mark. Most 'contradictory sources' cases resolve this way: not one winner, but a discovery that the sources were never measuring the same thing.

Probe the boundary densely — just below, exactly at, and just above — because bracket logic lives or dies at its edges:

The tester is right, and the probes show two distinct faults at the boundary:

49999 -> tool: 4999.900000000001 | correct: 4999.900000000001
50000 -> tool: 10000.0 | correct: 5000.0
50001 -> tool: 10000.2 | correct: 5000.2
60000 -> tool: 12000.0 | correct: 7000.0

First, the conceptual bug: above the threshold the tool taxes the entire income at 20%, while the stated rule taxes only the portion above $50,000 at 20% — at $60,000 the tool overstates the tax by $4,000. Second, the edge bug: the condition income >= 50000 means an income of exactly $50,000 is taxed $10,000 instead of $5,000 — the tax doubles for a one-dollar step across the line, the 'strange jump' the tester saw. At 49,999 the tool is right by accident, which is why casual testing missed it.

Boundary probing is the highest-yield verification for any rule with thresholds — tax brackets, discount tiers, age limits, free-shipping cutoffs. The doctrine: for every threshold T in the specification, test T−1, T, and T+1, and also test the rule's intent at a large value where the two readings diverge unmistakably ($60,000 here separates '20% of everything' from '20% of the excess' by thousands). Specifications phrase brackets in prose ('on the portion above'), and prose-to-code translation is exactly where the portion gets lost. Verify the boundary, and you have verified the translation.

The simulation walks the balance down month by month — interest charged on what is actually owed, principal repaid by the rest — and accumulates $661.85 of interest, ending at a balance of zero, which is itself an invariant the simulation must satisfy. When the methods disagree, the simulation is the better diagnostic tool, because its month-by-month trace shows where the balance path bends away from expectation. This is the mature form of independent recomputation: not doing the same sum twice, but reaching the quantity through two different structures of reasoning and requiring them to meet.

Our warehouse system tags each bin label with a home-grown checksum: sum of the character codes, mod 256. Two different labels, 'BIN-AB' and 'BIN-BA', show the same checksum and caused a picking mix-up. Demonstrate why this checksum could not have caught the swap, and what property a better checksum needs.
Reproduce the collision exactly, then contrast with a position-sensitive checksum on the same pair:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
BIN-AB weak: 137 | weighted: 1347
BIN-BA weak: 137 | weighted: 1346
BIN-AC weak: 138 | weighted: 1353

The collision is structural, not bad luck:

BIN-AB weak: 137 | weighted: 1347
BIN-BA weak: 137 | weighted: 1346
BIN-AC weak: 138 | weighted: 1353

Addition is commutative — it does not care about order — so any rearrangement of the same characters sums identically. 'BIN-AB' and 'BIN-BA' are anagrams, and an order-blind checksum pronounces them identical. The weighted checksum, which multiplies each byte by its position, separates them immediately (and separates 'BIN-AC' too), because position is part of what it measures.

Every checksum has a collision class: a family of changes it cannot see. Mod-9 is blind to digit transposition and to errors that are multiples of 9; a plain sum is blind to all rearrangements; a length check is blind to everything except truncation. Verification design means matching the checksum's vision to the errors you actually fear. Warehouses fear swapped and transposed characters, so their checksums must be position-sensitive — as ISBN and Luhn already are, which is why their weights exist. The picking mix-up was not a checksum failure in the sense of a malfunction; the checksum performed exactly as designed. The failure was upstream, in choosing a check whose blind spot covered the most likely accident. Audit your checks against your accidents.

A project plan promises delivery in 10 days. Tasks: A (design, 3 days) must finish before B (build, 4 days) and C (content, 5 days); B and C must both finish before D (integration, 2 days); D before E (launch, 3 days). Verify the promise against the dependency graph.
A schedule's minimum duration is its longest dependency chain — the critical path. Computing every chain through the graph:

messages.content:
A earliest finish: day 3
B earliest finish: day 7
C earliest finish: day 8
D earliest finish: day 10
E earliest finish: day 13
project minimum duration: 13 days
promised: 10 days -> shortfall: 3 days

The promise is impossible — not risky, impossible:

A earliest finish: day 3
B earliest finish: day 7
C earliest finish: day 8
D earliest finish: day 10
E earliest finish: day 13
project minimum duration: 13 days
promised: 10 days -> shortfall: 3 days

The chain A → C → D → E alone consumes 3 + 5 + 2 + 3 = 13 days, and no management technique compresses a dependency chain below the sum of its links: integration cannot start before content exists, launch cannot precede integration. The plan is short by 3 days before a single thing goes wrong. The parallel chain through B takes 12 days, so C's chain is the critical one — C is where any rescue must happen (split it, start part of it before A fully finishes if the dependency is soft, or add resource to shorten it).

Verifying a schedule against its dependency graph is pure constraint checking, and it refutes a large class of project promises without any debate about estimates: even if every duration estimate is exactly right, the promise fails. That is the strongest kind of verification result — a proof of infeasibility from the plan's own numbers. When a deadline survives this check, the argument can move to estimates and risk, where judgement lives. When it does not, no amount of optimism, overtime rhetoric, or status meetings changes the arithmetic: the graph says 13, the promise says 10, and the graph wins.

In electrochemistry, an equation must balance atoms AND charge. Two claimed equations: (1) Fe + 2 H+ -> Fe2+ + H2, (2) Fe + 2 H+ -> Fe3+ + H2. Verify both against both invariants.
Two independent conservation laws, so two independent counts — an equation can pass one and fail the other:

def check(name, left_atoms, right_atoms, left_q, right_q):
    atoms_ok = left_atoms == right_atoms
    charge_ok = left_q == right_q
    print(f'{name}: atoms {left_atoms} vs {right_atoms} ->', 'OK' if atoms_ok else 'FAIL',
          f'| charge {left_q:+d} vs {right_q:+d} ->', 'OK' if charge_ok else 'FAIL')
check('Eq 1', {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2}, {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2}, 2, 2)
check('Eq 2', {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2}, {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2}, 2, 3)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:

Eq 2: atoms {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2} vs {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2} -> OK | charge +2 vs +3 -> FAIL

The two equations part company on the second invariant:

Eq 1: atoms {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2} vs {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2} -> OK | charge +2 vs +2 -> OK
Eq 2: atoms {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2} vs {'Fe': 1, 'H': 2} -> OK | charge +2 vs +3 -> FAIL

Equation 1 balances atoms and charge: two positive charges enter as hydrogen ions and leave carried by the iron ion, while the hydrogen departs neutral. It would need an electron on the right side to balance, and that electron's absence is the error.

Layered invariants are the mature form of conservation checking: a claim must satisfy every conservation law that applies to it, and passing one law says nothing about the others. The same structure appears in bookkeeping (a journal can balance debits while misclassifying accounts), in physics problems (an answer can conserve energy while violating momentum), and in data pipelines (row counts can match while checksums diverge). Verification checklists should therefore list invariants explicitly, one per line, each independently tested — because the human tendency is to stop at the first pass. Equation 2's author counted atoms, saw them match, and stopped. The charge was never counted. What is not on the checklist does not get checked; what does not get checked eventually gets published.

A tutoring company claims 'each extra hour of study adds 5 points to the test score.' Their own published data (hours, score): (1,52), (2,55), (3,61), (4,63), (5,69), (6,72). Verify the claim against the data by fitting the slope properly.

num = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in pts)
den = sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x, _ in pts)
slope = num / den

print('least-squares slope:', round(slope, 2), 'points per hour')
print('claimed: 5 points per hour')

The least-squares slope through their six points is about 4.11 points per hour, not 5 — the marketing figure inflates the measured relationship by roughly a fifth. A student trusting the claim budgets four hours for a 20-point gain the data prices at five hours.

Our audit journal chains its entries: each entry's hash covers the previous hash plus its own content, so tampering should be detectable. Recompute the chain from genesis using the stored content, and compare each recomputed link with the hash stored at the time — the first mismatch is where history was rewritten:

import hashlib
def link(prev, text):
    return hashlib.sha256((prev + '|' + text).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
original = ['deposit 500', 'fee 45', 'transfer 1200', 'withdrawal 300']
stored = []
h = 'GENESIS'
for t in original:
    h = link(h, t)
    stored.append(h)
current = ['deposit 500', 'fee 45', 'transfer 200', 'withdrawal 300']
h = 'GENESIS'
for i, t in enumerate(current, 1):
    h = link(h, t)
    status = 'OK' if h == stored[i - 1] else 'MISMATCH'
    print(f'entry {i}: recomputed {h} vs stored {stored[i - 1]} -> {status}')

entry 2: recomputed d3a79c8cf42a vs stored d3a79c8cf42a -> OK

entry 4: recomputed 86e4a67b3e1c vs stored 9a9b0a577093 -> MISMATCH

The chain convicts entry 3 and clears entries 1 and 2:

entry 2: recomputed d3a79c8cf42a vs stored d3a79c8cf42a -> OK

entry 4: recomputed 86e4a67b3e1c vs stored 9a9b0a577093 -> MISMATCH

Entries 1 and 2 recompute to their stored hashes exactly. Entry 3 — whose content now reads 'transfer 200' — produces a different hash from the one stored when the entry was written, and entry 4 mismatches too, unavoidably: its stored hash was computed over the original entry 3, so the tamper poisons every subsequent link. That propagation is the design's genius and its diagnostic gift: the first mismatch localises the alteration to a single entry, while the cascade after it is expected fallout, not additional tampering.

Two honest limits complete the picture. The chain proves the journal was altered at entry 3; it does not prove what the original amount was (1200 is the allegation, and recovering it needs an external record — a bank statement, a counterparty's copy). And the chain only protects history if the stored hashes themselves are anchored somewhere the tamperer cannot rewrite — an external timestamp, a second copy, a published digest. A hash chain in a single editable file is a seal the forger can re-stamp. Verification architecture, like verification arithmetic, is about independence: the check must live outside the reach of the thing checked.

A retail chain reports: 'We redesigned the store layout in March and sales rose 15% in April. The redesign worked.' What would it take to actually verify that causal claim, and what else could explain the April rise?

The report verifies a sequence (redesign, then rise) and asserts a cause — and sequence is the weakest evidence for causation, because April differs from March in more ways than the layout. Rival explanations queue up immediately: seasonality (April brings Easter, warmer weather, and garden season for many retailers — March-to-April rises happen in years with no redesign at all); a promotion or advertising campaign running concurrently; a competitor's closure nearby; payday and holiday timing; even weather on the specific weekends. Each rival predicts the same 15% rise without the layout doing anything.

What would settle it is a comparison that holds the rivals still. The strongest practical design: the chain has other stores — compare redesigned stores against similar non-redesigned stores over the same months (if the untouched stores also rose 13%, the layout's contribution is about 2 points, not 15). Weaker but useful: compare against the same stores' March-to-April change in previous years, establishing the seasonal baseline the claim must beat. And check the mechanism's fingerprint: a layout effect should appear in layout-sensitive measures (dwell time, basket size, sales in the re-zoned departments) before it appears in totals; a pure seasonal lift raises everything evenly, including departments the redesign never touched.

Until such a comparison exists, the verified statement is only 'sales rose 15% in April, after a March redesign' — a chronology, not a cause. Causal claims are verified by eliminating rivals, not by accumulating confirming instances, and the discipline of listing rivals first is what separates an analyst from a press release.
A student derived a pendulum period formula T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) but isn't sure they didn't flip it to sqrt(g / L). Verify the formula without looking it up — using units and behaviour.
Two independent probes: dimensional analysis (the result must come out in seconds), and a scaling probe (quadrupling L must do something specific and checkable):

The student's formula is the right way up, and both probes confirm it. Dimensionally: L/g has units of metres divided by metres-per-second-squared, which is seconds squared; its square root is seconds — a period. The flipped version, g/L, has units of 1/seconds², whose root is 1/seconds — a frequency, not a period. The unit check alone settles the orientation without any reference book.

The scaling probe adds behavioural evidence: for L = 1 m the formula gives T ≈ 2.01 s, matching the well-known near-two-second swing of a metre pendulum (the historical basis of the seconds pendulum). Quadrupling the length to 4 m gives 4.01 s — exactly double, as a square-root law demands: period grows with the square root of length, so 4× the length means 2× the period. Had the formula been flipped, a longer pendulum would swing faster, contradicting every playground swing ever observed — long swings are slow. Verification by units and by limiting behaviour is how physicists audit formulas before trusting their numbers: the formula must have the right dimensions, the right extremes, and the right scaling, and a formula that passes all three has very little room left to be wrong.

We're migrating three tables (customers, orders, payments) to a new database next weekend. Present a verification plan as a table: for each check, what it compares, the pass criterion, and what failure would mean. We can afford row counts, column checksums, and a 1% sample join — not a full manual review.

Verification plan for the migration — every check compares the target against the source, and no check trusts the migration tool's own log:

| # | Check | Comparison | Pass criterion | A failure means |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Row counts | COUNT(*) per table, source vs target | Exactly equal, all three tables | Rows dropped or duplicated in transfer |
| 2 | Monetary checksums | SUM(amount) per money column, to the cent | Exactly equal | Silent rounding, currency, or truncation errors |
| 3 | Key integrity | COUNT of duplicate primary keys in target | Zero duplicates | Key collisions merged distinct records |
| 4 | Referential integrity | Payments whose order_id has no matching order (and the reverse) | Zero orphans beyond the source's own known orphans | Broken relationships after re-keying |
| 5 | Extremes audit | MIN/MAX of dates and amounts per table | Equal on both sides | Range-based filters quietly excluded edge rows (first/last day, zero amounts) |
| 6 | Sample join | Random 1% of customers joined to their orders and payments, field-by-field | Every sampled field identical | Encoding, timezone, or type-conversion drift that aggregates hide |
| 7 | Null census | COUNT of NULLs per nullable column | Equal per column | Defaults swallowed missing data, or missing data invented defaults |

The plan is layered by failure mode: counts catch loss, checksums catch alteration, extremes catch boundary exclusion, and the sample join catches the semantic drift — shifted timezones, mangled characters, decimals stored as floats — that totals cannot see because they net out or never touch the affected fields. Two disciplines make it a verification rather than a ritual: the checks run against the source as ground truth (never against the migration report, which is the system grading its own homework), and the pass criteria are written down before the migration runs, so a tired team at 2 a.m. cannot negotiate a failure into a pass. Sign-off requires every row green; any red row names its own investigation.
A service report states: 'mean response time 240 ms (95% CI: 225 to 255 ms), based on a sample of 36 requests with standard deviation 45 ms.' Verify the interval from the summary statistics.
A confidence interval is a derived figure with a strict recipe — mean plus/minus roughly 1.96 standard errors — so re-derive it from n and the SD:

arguments.code:
import math
n, mean, sd = 36, 240.0, 45.0
se = sd / math.sqrt(n)
margin = 1.96 * se
print('standard error:', se)
print('margin:', round(margin, 1))
print('recomputed 95% CI:', round(mean - margin, 1), 'to', round(mean + margin, 1))
print('reported CI: 225 to 255')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
standard error: 7.5
margin: 14.7
recomputed 95% CI: 225.3 to 254.7
reported CI: 225 to 255

The interval verifies:

standard error: 7.5
margin: 14.7
recomputed 95% CI: 225.3 to 254.7
reported CI: 225 to 255

The standard error is 45 / √36 = 7.5 ms, the margin is 1.96 × 7.5 ≈ 14.7 ms, and the recomputed interval (225.3 to 254.7) rounds to the reported 225–255. Whoever produced the report ran the standard recipe with the standard multiplier.

Two deeper checks are worth modelling while we are here. First, plausibility of the inputs: a standard deviation of 45 on a mean of 240 is a coefficient of variation under 20% — reasonable for response times, though real latency data is usually right-skewed, which would make a symmetric interval a simplification worth a footnote. Second, interpretation: the interval is a claim about the mean's precision, not a promise that 95% of requests fall between 225 and 255 ms — individual requests vary by the full SD of 45, and readers who mistake the CI for the data's range will be surprised by every slow request. Verifying a statistic has three layers — arithmetic, assumptions, interpretation — and a figure can pass the first while failing the third in the reader's head. The report's arithmetic is clean; if you quote it, quote it as a statement about the average, which is all it ever was.

A project bid is priced at $46,950. Its work breakdown: design 18,500, build 12,300, testing 9,750, deployment 6,400. The resource plan says: 320 senior hours at $85, 210 junior hours at $70, materials $5,050. A previous similar project cost $44,000 and this one is scoped about 8% larger. Verify the bid by all three routes.
Three structurally different estimates — bottom-up by work package, bottom-up by resources, and top-down by analogy — should triangulate on the same neighbourhood:

Two routes agree exactly and the third lands within 1.2%. By work package: $46950. By resources: 320 × 85 = 27,200, plus 210 × 70 = 14,700, plus materials 5,050 gives $46950 — identical, which is a real cross-check because the two breakdowns were assembled along different axes (deliverables versus inputs) and a costing error would have to be duplicated in both to survive. By analogy: $44,000 scaled by 8% gives $47520, which is $570 above the bid — close enough to corroborate the order of magnitude, far enough to be a conversation about whether the 8% scope growth was estimated honestly.

Triangulation between estimation methods is how experienced estimators sanity-check a number that cannot be 'looked up': no single method is trusted, and the spread between methods is itself information — a bid where the routes spread by 30% is a bid nobody understands yet, whatever its total says. Note the asymmetry of the verdicts: the two bottom-up routes verify the bid's internal consistency (the price is the sum of its stated parts, twice over), while only the analogy route tests it against the world (what similar work actually cost). Internal agreement plus external plausibility is the complete verification; either alone is half.

A puzzle book claims that n^2 + n + 41 gives a prime number for every whole number n. It lists n=1 to n=10, all prime. Verify the universal claim as far as computation reasonably can, and report honestly what verification can and cannot do here.
A universal claim over infinitely many n cannot be proven by examples — but it can be refuted by one. Testing every n up to 60:

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
first failure at n = 40 value = 1681
factorisation: 1681 = 41 x 41
all n from 0 to 39 give primes — 40 consecutive confirmations

The claim is false, and the manner of its failure is the lesson:

first failure at n = 40 value = 1681
factorisation: 1681 = 41 x 41
all n from 0 to 39 give primes — 40 consecutive confirmations

The formula produces primes for forty consecutive values of n — an extraordinary run that would convince anyone testing casually — and then fails at n = 40, where the value is 1681 = 41 × 41. The failure is not a coincidence: at n = 40, the expression becomes 40² + 40 + 41, and at n = 41 every term is divisible by 41. The pattern was never a law; it was a long local regularity with a structural expiry date.

This is the purest demonstration of verification's asymmetry for universal claims. Confirmations accumulate without ever proving — forty successes, or forty thousand, leave the claim exactly as unproven as ten did, because the claim quantifies over infinitely many cases. A single counterexample, by contrast, is decisive forever. So the verifier's strategy for 'for all' claims is not to gather support but to hunt refutation, and to hunt where refutation is likeliest: at boundaries, at special values (here, n related to the constant 41), at the extremes of the claim's domain. The puzzle book's ten examples were chosen from the safest neighbourhood. Verification begins where the examples stop being convenient.

A numerical library reports the integral of x^2 from 0 to 1 as 0.3333. The exact answer is 1/3, but I want the library's numerical method itself verified, not just compared to the known answer — by an independent numerical method with a different error structure.

Approximate the integral twice: the midpoint rule and Simpson's rule, both at n = 1000. Their errors shrink at different rates and from different directions of bias, so agreement between them certifies the value independently of the exact answer:

arguments.code:
def midpoint(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    return h * sum(f(a + (i + 0.5) * h) for i in range(n))
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        s += (4 if i % 2 == 1 else 2) * f(a + i * h)
    return s * h / 3
f = lambda x: x * x
mid = midpoint(f, 0.0, 1.0, 1000)
sim = simpson(f, 0.0, 1.0, 1000)
print('midpoint rule:', round(mid, 8))
print('Simpson rule :', round(sim, 8))
print('difference   :', abs(mid - sim))
print('exact 1/3    :', round(1 / 3, 8))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
midpoint rule: 0.33333325
Simpson rule : 0.33333333
difference   : 8.333333312293689e-08
exact 1/3    : 0.33333333

The library's figure is certified by independent approximation:

midpoint rule: 0.33333325
Simpson rule : 0.33333333
difference   : 8.333333312293689e-08
exact 1/3    : 0.33333333

The midpoint rule gives 0.33333325 (a hair under 1/3, as theory predicts — for a convex function the midpoint rule underestimates slightly), and Simpson's rule, which fits parabolas instead of rectangles and converges far faster, lands on 0.33333333 to eight places. The two methods agree to about 8 × 10⁻⁸ despite sharing no code path, no formula, and no error term — the midpoint error scales as h², Simpson's as h⁴, so a bug or a mis-set limit in one would have to be mirrored by an unrelated coincidence in the other to survive.

This is the numerical analyst's version of independent recomputation, and its logic deserves stating plainly: when no exact answer exists — the normal case for real integrals — truth is approached by triangulation between methods whose errors are structurally different, and the gap between methods is your honest uncertainty. Report the value with that gap attached ('0.3333333 ± 1×10⁻⁷ by cross-method agreement') and you have said something both precise and defensible. A single method's output, however many digits it prints, carries no such warrant: digits are cheap; independent agreement is the evidence.

Errors cluster at boundaries because that is where conversions and conditions bite. Verify the boundaries, and the middle takes care of itself.

Claim A is false: August revenue (9,650) fell below July (9,800) — growth was not monthly, only quarterly-endpoint to endpoint. Claim C is false: returns rose every month, 310 → 355 → 402, both in dollars and as a share of revenue. Claim B is true: average order value rose from 46.67 to 52.78, a rise of about 13%.

And claim B is where the real verification begins, because its truth is doing misleading work. Order value rose while orders fell (210 → 198) and returns climbed — the pattern of a shop losing its small, ordinary customers and keeping a shrinking base of large ones, with worsening product satisfaction. The same table that verifies B refutes the health story B was recruited to tell. A summary assembled from one true clause and two false ones, arranged so the true clause carries the impression, is worse than an honest bad quarter: the falsehoods borrow credibility from the verified fact.

The mature verification habit is therefore two-stage. Stage one, per-claim: recompute every clause, as here. Stage two, per-impression: ask what conclusion a reasonable reader would take from the whole, and check that conclusion against the data too. Documents fail stage two more often than stage one, because stage two has no formula — only the discipline of reading your own summary as an adversary would, then returning to the table to see if the table agrees with the feeling the prose creates.

An AI tool generated a market summary for us. It claims: (1) the total market is $4.3B, from segments A $1.2B, B $0.8B, C $2.1B; (2) the market grew 14% year over year, from $3.6B; (3) segment C is the largest segment. Run a verification protocol over the summary — don't just answer, show the protocol working.
The protocol: extract every checkable claim, classify it (sum, ratio, superlative), execute the check for each, and issue a verdict per claim — no global impressions:

arguments.code:
segments = {'A': 1.2, 'B': 0.8, 'C': 2.1}
total = sum(segments.values())
print('CLAIM 1 — stated total 4.3 | recomputed:', round(total, 2), '->', 'PASS' if abs(total - 4.3) < 0.001 else 'FAIL')
growth = (total - 3.6) / 3.6 * 100
print('CLAIM 2 — stated growth 14% | recomputed from segments:', round(growth, 1), '% ->', 'PASS' if abs(growth - 14) < 0.5 else 'CHECK BASIS')
growth_claimed_total = (4.3 - 3.6) / 3.6 * 100
print('        growth implied by the stated total:', round(growth_claimed_total, 1), '%')
largest = max(segments, key=segments.get)
print('CLAIM 3 — largest segment stated as C | computed largest:', largest, '->', 'PASS' if largest == 'C' else 'FAIL')

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
CLAIM 1 — stated total 4.3 | recomputed: 4.1 -> FAIL
CLAIM 2 — stated growth 14% | recomputed from segments: 13.9 % -> PASS
        growth implied by the stated total: 19.4 %
CLAIM 3 — largest segment stated as C | computed largest: C -> PASS

The protocol's verdict sheet:

CLAIM 1 — stated total 4.3 | recomputed: 4.1 -> FAIL
CLAIM 2 — stated growth 14% | recomputed from segments: 13.9 % -> PASS
        growth implied by the stated total: 19.4 %
CLAIM 3 — largest segment stated as C | computed largest: C -> PASS

Claim 1 fails: the segments sum to 4.1, not 4.3 — the summary's headline total is inconsistent with its own segment table by 0.2B. Claim 3 passes cleanly. Claim 2 is the subtle one: 14% growth is consistent with the recomputed total of 4.1 (13.9%), but wildly inconsistent with the summary's own stated total of 4.3 (which would imply 19.4% growth). So the growth figure and the segment table agree with each other, and the headline total is the lone error — probably a stale figure from an earlier draft, surviving while everything around it was updated.

That pattern — two parts of a document corroborating each other against a third — is cross-verification inside a single source, and it is the working core of the protocol this record demonstrates. Step one: extract claims mechanically; a claim you cannot state as a checkable proposition ('the market is dynamic') is marked unverifiable and set aside, not absorbed. Step two: classify each claim — sums get re-added, ratios get re-divided, superlatives get ranked, trends get re-plotted from the underlying series. Step three: execute, with the document's own numbers first (internal consistency) and external sources after (correspondence). Step four: verdict per claim, in writing, with the recomputed value beside the stated one. AI-generated text needs this protocol more than most sources, not because it errs more, but because it errs fluently — the prose gives no signal about which figures were computed and which were confabulated. The protocol supplies the signal. Run it on every summary, whoever or whatever wrote it.
